Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.
Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).
The short version
Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.
What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home?
Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:
- A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup.
- Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth.
- An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section.
That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.
Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run?
It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.
On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.
What Is Quantization?
Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.
The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.
If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.
Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM?
For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.
Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.
If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs.
If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.
Small
  8-12 GB
  UD-Q4_K_S or Q4_K_M
  8K-16K
Medium
  16 GB
  Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE)
  Q4_K_M or Q5_K_M
  16K-32K
Large
  24 GB
  UD-Q4_K_M or Q4_K_S
  16K-32K
Extra Large
  32 GB+
  UD-Q4_K_XL or Q6_K
  64K-128K+
Models marked MoE (mixture of experts) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way.
Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate.
Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090?
Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.
Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.
Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.
2-bit
  10-11 GB
  12 GB card
3-bit
  13-15 GB
  16 GB card
4-bit (recommended)
  17-18 GB
  24 GB card
8-bit (lossless)
  24 GB
  32 GB card
Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.
Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station, not a graphics card.
Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac?
Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory. Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon.
The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark.
How Do You Set Up a Local AI with Unsloth Desktop?
It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along.
Step 1: Install Unsloth Desktop
First, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup.
I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription.
The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor.
Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one.
Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded.
Step 2: Download a Quantized Model
On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B.
The model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list.
You should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU.
Every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting.
Step 3: Set the Context Size
Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need.
I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU.
At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth.
Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup.
How Do You Share a Local AI Across Your Home Network?
Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network.
Once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC.
Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab.
Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part.
Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set.
Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it.
Can You Access Your Local AI Across the Internet? Soon™
Not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network.
If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away.
In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship.
As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help.
PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go!
Sources
  Free, open-source app for macOS, Windows and Linux; runs GGUF and MLX models
  Remote & LAN settings, LAN access start and port behaviour
  Official 16-bit weights (~56 GB) and parameter count
  Quantized files and sizes, including UD-Q4_K_XL (~18 GB)
  26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, 1M context, UD-Q4_K_XL at 17.6 GB, memory by precision
  594B parameters, smallest file 171.7 GB
  Official weights, released November 17, 2026
  32 GB GDDR7 consumer GPU used for this build

articles.title: Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
articles.body:
Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates, and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees, a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you.
Tech leaders are celebrating Jensen Huang’s return
Huang is getting by with a little help from his friends.
Elon Musk, for one, is thrilled.
And why wouldn’t he be? As a fellow leather jacket enthusiast who has a checkered history with women — including those who work for him — it’s clear that he and Huang have a lot in common beyond their positions as tech CEOs. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, too, is a man who can relate to Huang’s struggle.
Gavin Baker, founder and chief investment officer of Atreides, is so impressed by Huang’s rise from the ashes that he’s going to buy a leather jacket of his own.
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeny chimed in with an oblique reference to Huang’s outerwear.
And then there’s billionaire investor Bill Ackman, a real wife guy if there ever was one — but one who, for better or worse, seems to understand that the market comes first.
Of course, no one has been more effusive than the man who may have orchestrated it all. President Donald Trump posted his lengthy congratulations to Huang on Truth Social. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote. He commended Nvidia’s board for making the “correct and proper” decision in reinstating Huang — a decision that, the board admits, was made with input “from senior levels of the United States government,” who determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no security risk.” Isn’t that great news?
Trump expects Huang to make him proud. “I think you’re going to see some tremendous numbers out of this company,” Trump said on CNBC. “I talked to him last night. I said, ‘Jensen, just promise me one thing: You’re going to work hard.’ I spoke to him last night because I knew what was going on.”
The market’s reaction may be the most jubilant of all. Per Odd Lots host Joe Weisenthal, NASDAQ-100 futures jumped so quickly that trading was halted. Congratulations to everyone who bought the dip, I guess.

articles.title: US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades
articles.body:
US Intelligence Chief Predicts More Tech Outages As Systems Undergo Upgrades (reuters.com) 39
			
		 	
				Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages as companies and government agencies modernize aging infrastructure. Speaking on CNN, Clayton said the upgrades are necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity but will inevitably cause "glitches, gaps, [and] interruptions in service." Reuters reports:  A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical U.S. systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network.
Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course."   Clayton told CNN: "The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road."
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning on CBS News' Face the Nation: "I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn't the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks ... The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now."

articles.title: White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
articles.body:
It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor. “We have to protect our geniuses.”
White House brags that Trump was ‘totally involved’ in getting Jensen reinstated
Trump said Nvidia’s board ‘made the correct and proper decision’ to bring back Jensen Huang.
Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.”
Trump also said, “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.”
Nvidia said in its announcement that its board “received input from senior levels of the United States government” that made them confident reinstating Huang would not pose a national security risk, following reports about his involvement with an alleged Chinese spy.
Trump also posted on Truth Social that Nvidia’s board “made the correct and proper decision” to reinstate Huang, adding:
“The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
Less than 12 hours earlier, Trump said in a separate post that Huang’s reinstatement “would be the best thing” for Nvidia and the US, and urged the board to rehire him. Reporting from Semafor now says that he was calling in to Nvidia’s board meeting around this time to make the same argument.

articles.title: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file
articles.body:
NariQ: Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file, BF16-level on long-horizon agentic tasks
(Nov 20, 2026) We are releasing NariQ v1 GGUFs of Qwen3.8-27B at 3, 2.5 and 2 bits per weight. Run them on our llama.cpp fork (required).
- The 3-bit and 2.5-bit files match BF16 on long-horizon agent tasks, math and image understanding. The 2-bit file scores lower.
- NariQ is a trellis-coded post-training quantization (PTQ), calibrated on real coding-agent traces and stored in a layout that runs on a single GPU.
- More details are in the tech report.
Each cell gives a percentage and a count in parentheses. For DeepSWE, the count is the mean number of fully solved tasks per round. Across the same three rounds, the mean share of each task's new tests that passed was 83.1% (BF16), 82.9% (3-bit), 83.2% (2.5-bit) and 77.2% (2-bit). One BF16 verifier timeout in round 3 counts as zero (338 of 339 trials graded). Each NariQ variant had all 339 trials graded. Terminal-Bench counts solved trials, and the remaining columns count correct answers. The agent runs use the Claude Code CLI (2.1.309, thinking on, effort max) driving the local model, with a 262,144-token context and the model's thinking-mode sampling (temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 20).
KL divergence from the BF16 model on held-out coding-agent traces, against file size. Every point was measured by us with the same code. Lower is better.
DeepSWE fully solved tasks out of 113, against file size. Our NariQ points and solid BF16 line average three rounds with Claude Code. Our GSQ-RCO points use one round. The hollow diamonds show approximate averages from Unsloth's published Dynamic V3.1 chart (mini-swe-agent). Compare each point with the BF16 line for its harness. Higher is better.
Terminal-Bench 2.1 score over 82 tasks × 3 attempts, against file size. Filled circles are our runs (Claude Code); hollow diamonds are Unsloth's reported results (mini-swe-agent), read from its published Dynamic V3.1 chart (hence ≈; its scores are averages over several passes). The two harnesses differ, so compare each point with the BF16 line of its own harness (solid: ours, dashed: Unsloth's). Higher is better.
Quickstart
One command on Linux with an NVIDIA GPU and driver 570 or newer (downloads the fork's binaries and the files, checks them, and fits the context to your GPU):
curl -fsSLO https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp/releases/download/b12431-nariv0/run.sh
bash run.sh 3.0   # or 2.5, 2.0
Or download and serve yourself, with llama-server from the fork:
hf download nari-labs/Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-GGUF \
    Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-3.0bpw.gguf Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-mmproj-BF16.gguf --local-dir .
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-3.0bpw.gguf --mmproj Qwen3.8-27B-NariQ-mmproj-BF16.gguf \
    -ngl 99 -c 131072 --jinja --port 8080 \
    --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 --min-p 0
The sampling flags are the thinking-mode settings our scores used. -c 131072 fits a 24 GB GPU with little to spare;
lower it if a display shares the GPU, or let run.sh pick the largest context that fits. Use -c 262144 (the model's
full context) on 32 GB or more. GPU memory with the vision projector:
Prebuilt binaries, the Docker image, supported GPUs and build steps: the fork's README.
Decode speed on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell), single session, 512 greedy output tokens, tokens/s:
NariQ on our llama.cpp fork with -fa on -ctk bf16 -ctv bf16 -t 1 -tb 16 --backend-sampling --samplers temperature (greedy sampling on the GPU, BF16 KV cache). UD-IQ3_XXS is Unsloth's file on llama.cpp, measured earlier on the same GPU type.
Known limits and future work
- Requires a NariQ-aware runtime: for now, our llama.cpp fork. Stock llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio can't load the new tensor types yet; we hope to merge support into upstream llama.cpp. Our internal SGLang plugin and our inference engine built on Resin are a work in progress for potential public release.
- The llama.cpp fork needs more work across hardware. The current fork is focused on SM120 performance (e.g. RTX PRO 6000). Ampere, Ada and Hopper GPUs and Apple M-series GPUs are slower than comparable GGUFs for now; we would love open-source contributions for speedups, as this has been a solo effort. GPUs older than Ampere fall back to slow CPU execution, and AMD and Intel GPUs are not supported yet. GeForce cards have not been tested yet; tested GPUs are RTX PRO 6000, H100, L4 and A10.
- Apple M-series (Metal): build from source; on an M3 Pro (18 GB) decode is about 3.8 tok/s with the 3.0bpw file (4.9 with 2.0bpw), far slower than CUDA. Other Macs are untested.
- The 2-bit file is weaker overall; use the 2.5-bit or 3-bit for higher overall performance.
- The vision tower stays in BF16; only the language model is quantized. The MTP (multi-token prediction) module is not included yet; it is still to be quantized.
- KV-cache and activation quantization are next, so the files fit long contexts on 16 GB consumer GPUs and run faster. Today the KV cache and activations stay in BF16.
Contact us
For technical consulting, compute sponsorships, or partnership inquiries, please contact founders@narilabs.com.
License
These files inherit the base model's Apache-2.0 license; see NOTICE.
Acknowledgements
Thanks to the Qwen team for the amazing Qwen3.8-27B, and to the Unsloth, ExLlamaV3, GSQ-RCO (IST Austria DASLab) and GGML teams, whose open-source work this release builds on. NariQ's trellis codes build on QTIP (Tseng et al., 2024).
Citation
If you use NariQ, please cite the technical report:
@techreport{kim2026nariq,
  title       = {NariQ: Sub-3-Bit Quantization for Long-Horizon Agentic Tasks},
  author      = {Doyeob (Toby) Kim},
  institution = {Nari Labs},
  year        = {2026},
  month       = nov,
  eprint      = {2611.26157},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  url         = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26157}
}
Qwen3.8-27B
Following the widespread community adoption of the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 series, we are pleased to introduce Qwen3.8, the most capable generation in the Qwen open-model family to date.
Built on the architectural foundation of Qwen3.5, Qwen3.8 delivers substantial gains across coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks. Qwen3.8-27B brings these advances to a compact, deployment-friendly dense model: a native vision-language model that understands images and videos, with flexible thinking control, designed to carry complex, multi-step tasks through to completion with greater reliability.
Qwen3.8 Highlights
Qwen3.8-27B features the following enhancements:
- Core Capabilities: Comprehensive improvements across coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic tasks.
- Agent Execution: Stronger autonomous planning and better handling of environment feedback, leading to more reliable end-to-end task completion.
- Downstream Compatibility: Broader support for popular harnesses and development tools, making it easier to integrate into your existing stack.
- Flexible Thinking Control: Thinking mode is on by default and can be disabled per request; reasoning depth can be tuned with reasoning_effort, and reasoning context from historical messages is retained via preserve_thinking.
- Vision-Language Understanding: Native support for image and video understanding, from STEM diagrams and documents to hour-scale videos.
Model Overview
- Type: Causal Language Model with Vision Encoder
- Training Stage: Pre-training & Post-training
- Language Model
  - Number of Parameters: 27B
  - Hidden Dimension: 5120
  - Token Embedding: 248,320 (Padded)
  - Number of Layers: 64
  - Hidden Layout: 16 × (3 × (Gated DeltaNet → FFN) → 1 × (Gated Attention → FFN))
  - Gated DeltaNet:
    - Number of Linear Attention Heads: 48 for V and 16 for QK
    - Head Dimension: 128
  - Gated Attention:
    - Number of Attention Heads: 24 for Q and 4 for KV
    - Head Dimension: 256
    - Rotary Position Embedding Dimension: 64
  - Feed Forward Network:
    - Intermediate Dimension: 17,408
  - LM Output: 248,320 (Padded)
  - MTP (Multi-Token Prediction): trained with multiple steps
- Context Length: 262,144 natively and extensible up to 1,000,000 tokens.
Best Practices
To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following settings:
- Sampling Parameters: We suggest using the following sets of sampling parameters: 
  - Thinking Mode: temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=0.0, repetition_penalty=1.0
  - Instruct (or non-thinking) mode: temperature=0.7, top_p=0.80, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0
 For supported frameworks, you can adjust the presence_penalty parameter between 0 and 2 to reduce endless repetition. However, using a higher value may occasionally result in language mixing and a slight decrease in model performance.
- Adequate Output Length: To optimize performance on agentic tasks, we recommend allocating sufficient output length to allow the model to generate detailed and comprehensive responses. For frameworks that support separate token limits for internal reasoning and final outputs, we suggest the following configuration within the 1M context length: 
  - Reasoning Content: Set the maximum output length to 262,144 tokens.
  - Final Response: Set the maximum output length to 131,072 tokens.
These settings provide the necessary capacity for complex reasoning while ensuring ample space for high-quality final deliverables.
- Processing Ultra-Long Texts: Qwen3.8-27B natively supports context lengths of up to 262,144 tokens. For long-horizon tasks where the total length (including both input and output) exceeds this limit, we recommend using RoPE scaling techniques to handle long texts effectively, e.g., YaRN.
- Long Video Understanding: To optimize inference efficiency for plain text and images, the size parameter in the released video_preprocessor_config.json is conservatively configured. It is recommended to set the longest_edge parameter in the video_preprocessor_config file to 469,762,048 (corresponding to 224k video tokens) to enable higher frame-rate sampling for hour-scale videos and thereby achieve superior performance. For example,
{"longest_edge": 469762048, "shortest_edge": 4096}
Alternatively, override the default values via engine startup parameters. For implementation details, refer to: vLLM / SGLang.
Citation
@misc{qwen38,
    title = {{Qwen3.8-Max}: A New Bar for Coding and Cowork},
    url = {https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3.8},
    author = {{Qwen Team}},
    month = {August},
    year = {2026}
}
- Downloads last month
  2,243
We're not able to determine the quantization variants.

articles.title: A Partial Evaluator for C
articles.body:
Tempo Specializer - A Partial Evaluator for C
What is Tempo?
Partial evaluation is program
transformation that automates a program
specialization process. Tempo is a
partial evaluator for C programs. It has been applied in various
domains such as operating systems and networking, computer graphics, scientific
computation, software engineering and domain specific languages. A first
workshop on Tempo has been organized in March 1998.
Tempo is now being distributed. Its documentation
is available on line, as well as tutorial
slides.
An Overview of Tempo
Tempo is a partial
evaluator for C programs. It is being developed in the Compose
project at IRISA / INRIA - LABRI
(France).
Tempo is an off-line specializer; it is divided into two phases:
analysis and specialization.
The input to the analysis phase consists of a program and a description
of which inputs will be known during specialization and which will be unknown.
Based on this knowledge, dependency analyses propagate information about
known and unknown values throughout the code and produce an annotated program,
indicating how each program construct should be transformed during specialization.
Because C is an imperative language including pointers, the analysis phase
performs alias and side-effect analyses in addition to binding-time
analyses. The accuracy of these analyses is targeted towards keeping
track of known values across procedures, data structures, and pointers.
Following the analysis phase, the specialization phase generates a specialized
program based on the annotated program and the values of the known inputs.
Tempo can specialize programs at compile time (i.e.,
source-to-source tranformation) as well as run time
(i.e., run-time binary code generation).
For more details, please consider reading some of our papers, most of which
are available at the following URL: papers.
Program Analysis
As a first step, the user provides a program and specifies what arguments
(including global variables) are static. For example, the user provides
the following code for a miniprintf function, and specifies in
this way that the first argument is static whereas the second is dynamic:
miniprintf(S,D).
miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[])
{
  int i = 0;
  while( *fmt != '\0' ) {
    if( *fmt != '%' )
       putchar(*fmt);
    else
      switch(*++fmt) {
        case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;             
        case '%' : putchar('%');     break;
        default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;
      }
    fmt++;
  }
}
From this Tempo produces a program file with analysis annotations.
These annotations can be visualized using colors that highlight the propagation
of the known/unknown information throughout the program.
/*  LEGEND:  STATIC  DYNAMIC
 */
miniprintf(char fmt[], int val[])
{
  int i = 0;
  while( *fmt != '\0' ) {
    if( *fmt != '%' )
       putchar(*fmt);
    else
      switch(*++fmt) {
        case 'd' : putint(val[i++]); break;              
        case '%' : putchar('%');     break;
        default  : prterror(*fmt);   break;
      }
    fmt++;
  }
}
The blue color (bold face for black and white display) represent static
constructions, i.e. values that can be computed at specialization
time. The red color (standard font for black and white display) is for
dynamic expressions, whose value cannot be precomputed knowing only the
static arguments. Basically, everything in blue (bold) will disappear after
specialization; only red (standard font) parts will remain.
The visualization of the analysis is very important for the user to
assess the amount of specialization in the code. Furthermore, the analysis
speeds up the specialization process (as opposed to
on-line partial
evaluators). The analysis is inter-procedural and takes into account pointer
aliases and side-effects.
Compile-Time Specialization
When the user is satisfied with the analysis (i.e., what the user
expects to specialize indeed appears as static), actual specialization
values must be provided. For example, giving
"<%d,%d>" as the
actual specialization value for the fmt argument of the miniprintf()
function yields the following specialized code.
miniprintf_1(int val[])
{
  putchar( '<'    );
  putint ( val[0] );
  putchar( ','    );
  putint ( val[1] );
  putchar( '>'    );
}
Many specializations can be made, sharing the same analysis. Only different
specialization values have to be provided.
Runtime Specialization
Tempo can also perform runtime specialization, using optimized binary code
templates. A dedicated runtime specializer is generated from the analysis
of the program. In the case of the
miniprintf function, Tempo
generates a runtime specializer rts_miniprintf_1() which can be
used as in the following example.
/*
 * Some dynamic execution context for variable 'format'
 */
spec_printf = rts_miniprintf_1(format);
...
(*spec_printf)(val1);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val1) */
(*spec_printf)(val2);   /* <=> miniprintf(format,val2) */
The function rts_miniprintf_1() is a dedicated runtime specializer.
It returns a pointer to the specialized function. Several specialized versions
can also be generated and used at the same time.
Applications of Tempo
Tempo has been successfully applied in various domains, yielding substantial
speedups.
- 
Operating system and networking:
  - 
Sun RPC, Chorus IPC, BSD packet filter, Unix signals, active networks,
- 
Computer graphics (various filtering algorithms),
- 
Scientific computation (trajectory, FFT, math libraries),
- 
Software architectures and mechanisms:
  - 
Domain specific languages GAL, PLAN-P),
  - 
Selective broadcast (implicit invocation),
  - 
Pattern matching,
  - 
Interpreters,
  - 
Software layers,
  - 
Generic libraries.
For an up-to-date list of non-confidential, published applications, please
browse our ``papers'' web page: papers.
Besides C, Tempo is currently being used as a back-end for specializing
Java programs using Harissa, a JavaVM-to-C compiler.
Fortran and C++ programs have also been specialized using translators to
C.
Projects Related to Tempo
- 
Cyclone
  
Cyclone is a mobile code system being developed as part of the
SwitchWare
active-network project at the University
of Pennsylvania. Cyclone uses two ideas to make mobile code safe as
well as fast: run-time code generation and proof-carrying code. Cyclone
relies on Tempo's analysis front-end (i.e. the binding-time analysis) and
on TAL/T, an extension of the TAL
typed assembly language.
Workshop
A workshop (actually closer to a ``winter
school'') on Tempo has been organized at IRISA,
March 16-18, 1998. The aim of this workshop was to present a three-day
tutorial on Tempo and its applications to real size programs. We had 24
participants, coming from universities as well as industries. We believe
it was a large success. The talks
are now available on-line.
Depending on request, if the distribution
of Tempo is a success, we might organize another workshop later. It would
less be like a ``winter school'' but rather like a real workshop with users
presenting applications and open discussions about possible improvements.
It would be preceded by an optional one-day tutorial for people not knowing
partial evaluation or Tempo.
Distribution
The Tempo specializer has been made publicly available under a licence
in April 1998. At of March 99, it was being used by about thirty people
around the world. The binary version of Tempo has just (July 2000) been
made available without any restrictions, and we expect a full unrestricted

Getting access to Tempo no longer requires signing a license agreement.
Tempo is simply available via anonymous FTP, as described below. In any

Tempo user. If you are, please also let us know if and for what purpose
you are using Tempo, by sending an email to tempo@labri.fr.
We will by default add you to our tempo talk mailing list tempo-talk@labri.fr,
where future Tempo releases will be announced, and Tempo users can discuss

What is Tempo?
Partial evaluation is program
transformation that automates a program
specialization process. Tempo is a

articles.title: Tesla’s FSD v15 turns driving visuals into Grand Theft Auto
articles.body:
Tesla has begun rolling out Full Self-Driving (Supervised) v15, calling it a ground-up overhaul of its end-to-end driver assist system. The centerpiece is Reality View, a real-time generative display that swaps out old wireframe graphics for a live, overhead camera angle that lets drivers see and tap to influence what the car plans to do next.
Tesla’s FSD v15 turns driving visuals into Grand Theft Auto
The update swaps blocky wireframes for a photorealistic overhead feed and promises a “25x” safety boost, even as federal regulators continue investigating the software.
The third-person perspective renders buildings, crosswalks, pedestrians, and surrounding traffic with a photorealism that has drawn immediate comparisons to Grand Theft Auto VI (which conveniently launched just days earlier). Even Elon Musk couldn’t resist the comparison on X, posting “FSD is GTA irl” shortly after the update dropped on Saturday.
Under the hood, FSD v15 runs on an upgraded vision encoder shared across Tesla’s FSD, Robotaxi, and Optimus humanoid robot programs. By training the model on millions of online videos, Tesla claims its AI learned to prevent serious driving mistakes 25 times more often while using less computing power. Of course, the update is built for vehicles running Tesla’s newer AI4 (HW4) hardware and upcoming Cybercab platforms, leaving millions of older HW3-equipped cars behind.
Beyond the flashy visuals, v15 packs several practical upgrades. A new Bike Rack Mode lets drivers engage FSD even with hitch accessories attached (though it disables reversing, Summon, and Autopark). The system can now automatically ease off the speed near traffic cameras, with an option to override and permanently mute specific cameras after two cancellations. Tesla also promises sharper hazard avoidance for potholes, standing water, and small animals, alongside smoother speed handling in school zones and bad weather.
Meanwhile, navigation learns preferred neighborhood routes and favorite parking spots over time, and the cabin camera can now track driver attention through hats and sunglasses while dialing back nagging alerts at higher speeds. Tesla has a pretty poor reputation for ensuring its drivers stay alert while using FSD, so hopefully this upgrade can improve that.
Still, Reality View raises an obvious question: is a hyper-detailed, video-game-style feed on the center touchscreen a helpful window into the car’s “brain,” or a tempting new distraction? For drivers who find the live feed overwhelming, Tesla includes a map-only option and a stripped-back “quiet mode”.
Tesla’s bold “25x” safety claim also lands amid intense federal scrutiny. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is actively investigating roughly 2.9 million FSD-equipped vehicles over reports of Teslas blowing through red lights, crossing railroad tracks improperly, and driving into oncoming lanes. Alongside dozens of cumulative fatalities linked to Tesla’s driver-assistance systems since 2019, the probe is a stark reminder of the gap between Tesla’s autonomous ambitions and a system that still legally requires a human to keep their eyes on the road.

articles.title: Google Search’s AI Mode can now tap into Drive and Wallet for more personalized responses
articles.body:
Google announced on Monday that it’s expanding Personal Intelligence in Search’s AI Mode with integrations for Google Drive, Google Wallet, and the Gemini app. Personal Intelligence is designed to offer users more personalized, context-aware answers by connecting to their Google apps and drawing on information from their digital lives. The feature can already connect to apps like Gmail, Google Calendar, and Google Photos.
By bringing Personal Intelligence in AI Mode to Drive, Wallet, and the Gemini app, Google is leveraging the wealth of user data that’s already within its ecosystem. Since users rely on these services, the tech giant can deliver more personalized experiences that rivals aren’t able to match. Of course, not everyone wants AI looking at their Wallet and Drive, so connecting the apps is optional, and you can turn Personal Intelligence on or off at any time.
Google says that connecting Google Wallet to Personal Intelligence lets users track their financial goals, cut everyday spending, and make better use of credit card rewards. The tech giant notes that if users choose to connect their Wallet, AI Mode can only read information from accounts and isn’t able to move or manage their money.
As for Drive, the company says important information related to a project or major decision is often scattered across documents and spreadsheets. By connecting Google Drive to Personal Intelligence, AI can draw on those files to provide more relevant, personalized answers, such as creating a tailored plan for tax season.
Users will also be able to share context between their Gemini app and AI Mode in Search, which means that if they explore an idea in the Gemini app, they won’t have to start over with AI Mode because it will already have the information, and vice versa.
Additionally, Google says users will soon be able to view the context AI Mode uses via a new “Personalization” icon that will appear below responses.
The company also announced on Monday that users will start to see more personally relevant responses in AI Overviews and AI Mode that will be tailored to users’ recent search context.

articles.title: One Man's Quest to End Daylight Savings
articles.body:
At a rally in Mississippi not long ago, Donald Trump complained about the reason for his frequent tardiness. “I’m always late. You know, I had a big meeting and I was an hour late. I said, ‘How?’ ” he told the crowd. “Daylight-saving time. We change it twice a year. . . . It’s ridiculous.” Trump has been urging the Senate to approve the Sunshine Protection Act—which was passed by the House in July and would make daylight-saving time permanent—before the bill expires at the end of the current Congress, on January 3rd.
His speech recalled an episode of HBO’s “Veep” in which Congressman Jonah Ryan is two hours late to a meeting after adjusting his clock the wrong way. “That’s impossible,” Ryan says. “I set my watch back for daylight-savings time. I springed backwards!” Told that he should have sprung forward, he’s irate: “Have you ever watched girls’ gymnastics? That makes no sense!”
“It’s a naturally funny topic,” Scott Yates said late last month, the day before the clocks were set back. Yates, a sixty-one-year-old former journalist, has spent a decade trying to end the changing of the clocks. “Some people plan their vacations around golf,” he said. “I use frequent-flier miles to fly to Michigan to testify.”
He was sitting outside a former chapel in Liberia, Costa Rica, to which he relocated from Colorado, in 2024. The country does not change the clocks. “It’s not the No. 1 reason I moved here, but it’s on the list,” he said. He wore Birkenstocks and no watch. Yates began his crusade after he read the book “A Complaint Free World.” “The idea is, if you can’t do something about it, you shouldn’t complain about it,” he said. “Robbing an hour of sleep just always annoyed me.” So he started a blog (locktheclock.net) in which he compiles research on the topic.
Yates found that studies linked the “spring forward” clock change—where people lose an hour of sleep—to a rise in heart attacks and medical incidents involving human error, while the “fall backward” clock change—where it gets dark earlier—led to an increase in fatal auto accidents. Both changes are associated with a spike in strokes.
Within a couple of years, legislators in more than a dozen states started contacting Yates about his writing. He’s helped draft bills, spoken at hearings, and, last year, testified before the Senate Commerce Committee, advocating to end clock changing. (His proposal would give states two years to decide which time to lock in.) He concluded his testimony with a story about how scientists often avoid changing lab rats’ schedules after a clock change because it disrupts results. “At long last, can we treat our citizens with the decency that we treat our lab rats?” he asked the senators.
Yates often gets e-mails from people with their own ideas about how to solve the problem. Computer programmers reach out suggesting that we stop using time zones and time changes altogether and put the whole world on Coördinated Universal Time, the international time standard. In New York, this might mean waking up at noon and having lunch at 6 P.M. “It’s never going to happen,” Yates said.
The idea of daylight-saving time was first implemented in Germany during the First World War, to save on energy costs, but it had built steam earlier in Europe as a health movement and was helped along by a golf-loving Englishman named William Willett, who liked to go riding early in the morning. “He was me a hundred years earlier,” Yates said. In 1907, Willett distributed a pamphlet called “The Waste of Daylight,” promoting a plan for four twenty-minute advances in the clock throughout the year. It went nowhere.
Around the same time, the National Baseball League wanted more light for evening games, while movie-theatre executives wanted less, thinking that darkness might drive people into cinemas. In the states, daylight-saving time was implemented as a fragmented system throughout the World Wars and assorted energy crises. In New York City, in 1951, Grand Central Terminal was home to two railroads that used different times. In the early sixties, there were twenty-three different combinations of start and end dates for daylight-saving time in Iowa alone. The Times described it as “time schizophrenia.” To remedy the clock anarchy, the Uniform Time Act of 1966 standardized the dates for daylight-saving time and gave states the option of moving to permanent Standard Time. Only Hawaii, Arizona (except the Navajo Nation), Puerto Rico, and a few other U.S. territories do not change the clocks.
“Time doesn’t exist,” Yates said. “The thing that we call time is just what we all agree on.” The Sunshine Protection Act is the closest he has come to getting his way, but the House bill is slightly different than what he advocated for. “Washington is just so dysfunctional,” he said. “If this was a thing with money behind it, it would’ve been worked out.” He added, “I’m so worried about Trump being in favor of it, because I don’t want to ruin it for another fifty years.” ♦

articles.title: Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
articles.body:
In separate but similar lawsuits filed on Monday, Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield and Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones accused SpaceX of violating state consumer protection laws by ignoring industry-standard safeguards and falsely promoting the safety of its X social media platform and Grok AI features. The complaint filed in Virginia accuses Musk of willfully ignoring growing concerns around AI-generated sexualized deepfakes, and “instead saw a market opportunity for more profits,” describing the weak safeguards around Grok as “not a failure but a feature.”
Oregon and Virginia sue SpaceX over Grok’s porn deepfakes
State AGs called the weak safeguards built into Elon Musk’s AI image generator ‘not a failure but a feature.’
“Time and again, xAI and X told consumers they were being protected from abuses. That was false. Instead, the tool permitted users to routinely create and circulate non-consensual intimate imagery and sexualized images, and child sexual abuse material (CSAM), causing harm to individuals and children,” Jones said in a press statement. “Companies that deploy powerful tools don’t get to ignore consumer safety and call it innovation.”
The complaints largely center around Grok Imagine, a tool that allows Grok and X users to generate images and videos. In August 2025, Grok maker xAI (which Musk has since merged with SpaceX) launched a “spicy” mode for Grok Imagine that spat out sexualized content including nude deepfakes of celebrities like Taylor Swift. In January 2026, Grok gained a feature that allowed X users to instantly edit any image without requiring consent from the original poster — resulting in X becoming flooded with nonconsensual, sexualized deepfakes of adults and minors.
xAI made several changes to restrict access to Grok image editing, moving some capabilities behind a paywall and blocking certain requests for sexual poses, swimwear, or explicit scenarios. Our testing at the Verge following these restriction updates found they did little to prevent the bot from creating sexualized deepfakes, however.
Both of the Oregon and Virginia lawsuits are seeking financial damages.
The X Safety team said in a statement released after the lawsuits were announced that it takes appropriate measures to address users who generate sexual content involving minors:
“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards. When some of these bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine earlier this year, we acted promptly to tighten its protections, which are designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people. To stay ahead of this disgusting and indefensible conduct, we keep testing and adjusting those protections as these abusers change tactics. We also implement sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt before an image is generated and check every output after.”

articles.title: What we learned operating auth for 1k APIs
articles.body:
In May 2025, we merged a PR at Nango that had a critical bug: an if condition that never fired prevented refreshed credentials from being saved to the database. We caught the bug and reverted it in just under two hours.
In those two hours, our scheduled jobs had refreshed and discarded access and refresh tokens for hundreds of connections. For most APIs, that was recoverable: the old refresh token still worked, so the next scheduled refresh repaired the connection.
Then we learned how many providers rotate refresh tokens.
Many providers, including Airtable and Atlassian, invalidate the old refresh token the moment a replacement is issued. Salesforce and Slack can do the same when rotation is enabled for the OAuth app.
There was no way to get those tokens back. For every affected connection, our customers had to ask their users to go through the consent screen again.
OAuth is a standard, but OAuth providers are not interchangeable. Each API’s auth behaves a little differently, and some of those differences are undocumented and only surface in production.
For context, Nango is an open-source project that lets web applications and agents integrate with third-party APIs. Our customers embed it in their products. Their users connect third-party accounts, and Nango keeps those connections working.
Since then, we’ve grown from supporting about 400 APIs to 1,000+ APIs. The incident changed how we operate auth, but it was only the first of several lessons.
Lesson 1: Token rotation makes ordinary bugs irreversible
Refresh token rotation is a security win, but a bug in the rotation path can permanently destroy a connection and force the user to reauthorize. That’s what made our incident so expensive.
We now treat refresh tokens like money, not cache. The new token gets persisted before anything else can fail. The persistence path has its own regression tests, and any platform-level refresh anomalies immediately page the on-call team.
Providers enforce refresh-token rotation differently
Take Airtable: a refresh request with a stale token or the wrong client credentials can return a 400 or 401, but Airtable doesn’t stop there. It revokes the user’s entire authorization for your app, and the only way back is for the user to reconnect. Sending the same refresh request twice can also cause revocation. Airtable documents a short grace period for duplicate refreshes, but retrying the stale token after that period revokes the authorization.
Airtable also invalidates the old access token the instant a refresh succeeds, so a long-running job still using an old token can fail mid-run.
Xero handles it better: if a refresh fails or the response never arrives, you can retry with the previous refresh token for up to 30 minutes.
Issues like these pushed us to serialize refreshes per connection behind a distributed lock.
*This is only the success path. Failure paths don’t fit in one diagram.
Even refreshing early can be wrong. For example, Exact Online’s access tokens last for 10 minutes, and its token endpoint rejects any refresh attempt made more than 30 seconds before expiry. Our “refresh 15 minutes early” rule meant every refresh fell outside that window and was rejected. We had to add support for per-provider expiration buffers.
Lesson 2: You can’t reliably know when access tokens expire
The official OAuth 2.0 spec (RFC 6749) makes expires_in optional for access tokens. For us, this has been a recurring source of silent breakage.
Zendesk, for example, rolled out expiring access tokens for OAuth clients, including existing ones. Its token response includes expires_in only if you request it. Without that parameter, the access token still expires under the default policy, but the response doesn’t say when. We discovered this only after the rotating refresh token lapsed and connections started dying.
Salesforce’s token response includes no expiry. The documented way to check it is a separate introspection endpoint, which we call before deciding whether to refresh an access token.
POST /services/oauth2/introspect HTTP/1.1
Host: yourInstance.my.salesforce.com
Authorization: Basic <base64 of client_id:client_secret>
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
token=<access_token>&token_type_hint=access_token
Sample response:
{
	"active": true,
	"scope": "id api refresh_token",
	"exp": 1549921091,
	"iat": 1549917491,
	"token_type": "Bearer",
	"client_id": "xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx"
}
But in June 2024, the introspection endpoint started intermittently returning unsupported_token_type for some tokens. When introspection failed, we refreshed anyway. The replacement access token could be introspected normally, though we never learned why the original token failed.
Refresh token lifetimes are just as inconsistent
- NetSuite’s OAuth refresh tokens expire after 7 days, requiring full re-consent, which is why many teams use its token-based authentication instead.
- Google’s refresh tokens live indefinitely, except under documented conditions, including the app being in “Testing” status, six months without use, or a user exceeding 100 live refresh tokens for your client.
We now refresh stale credentials on a cron, so tokens get exercised before inactivity kills them.
Auth failures don’t always look like failures
You’d expect an auth failure to return a 401. It often doesn’t:
- Zoho CRM’s token endpoint returns HTTP 200 with the error in the body.
- Workday and Dayforce return no error at all when a permission policy is missing; the API just returns empty data.
- One SOAP-based API we support returns HTTP 200 for everything, including wrong passwords.
- LastPass does the same, with the failure as plain text in the body. Our credential check for it literally searches the response for the string “Authorization Error”.
We ended up building per-provider heuristics: at the time of this analysis, 276 of the roughly 935 providers in our registry declared an authenticated endpoint that Nango can call to check whether credentials still work.
Lesson 3: Providers make breaking changes to their API auth
16% of commits to our provider config are fixes. There’s no reliable feed for provider auth changes; we often learn about them from a failed flow or a customer report.
Figma announced by email that credentials had to move from the request body to a Basic Authorization header and that the OAuth host was changing. We shipped the update, but anyone who missed the email might not discover the change until refreshes begin failing.
Shopify changed how offline tokens are issued, so apps began receiving expiring tokens where they previously didn’t. We shipped a config change to preserve the old behavior.
Lesson 4: Sometimes you build around the provider, not with it
Supporting a new API assumes two things: you can get credentials to test with, and you can find accurate docs for how its auth works. At our scale, both assumptions fail often enough that going around the provider is routine:
- Salesforce Data Cloud is separately provisioned, and none of our test orgs included it. Its auth requires two chained token exchanges against different hosts. We built a mock server from the documented responses so we could implement and test the flow without live credentials.
- LastPass’s API isn’t really REST: nearly every operation hits the same URL, with the action passed in the request body. That broke an assumption in our proxy that every integration would define individual endpoints, so we added support for APIs with only a base URL.
- A community member found the solution to a recurring Asana OAuth error (client_id is missing or invalid) in Asana’s support forum and added it to our docs. It wasn’t covered in Asana’s own docs.
- Read.ai’s documented authorization URL pointed at their internal developer-testing page. The real endpoint came from querying their OpenID discovery endpoint directly.
If you build an API, ten requests
API clients would fail less often if providers did these ten things:
- Return expires_in. Always, in seconds.
- If you rotate refresh tokens, consider a short, bounded grace period for the previous token, like Xero’s 30 minutes. This absorbs duplicate refreshes at the cost of weaker replay detection during that window.
- Return more specific errors than just invalid_grant. Revocation, policy failure, expired token: say which one it was in the error body.
- Treat auth changes as breaking API changes. Version them, announce them, and don’t apply them retroactively to existing clients.
- Document your revocation triggers. Password resets, per-user token caps, and inactivity windows.
- Offer some way to test against your API without a sales call (even for paid apps).
- Keep your auth documentation public and accurate.
- Make 200 mean success. If your API returns 200 OK with an error in the body, no generic client can tell it’s broken without special-casing your responses.
- Prefer conventional behavior when the specification leaves room for interpretation.
- If REST is your modern API, make it the source of truth. Don’t leave essential functionality only in SOAP or WSDL files.
Our provider registry is public in a single YAML file if you want to inspect the details.

articles.title: Sellers are Closing Etsy Stores in Response to Its New AI Training Policy
articles.body:
Sellers are Closing Etsy Stores in Response to Its New AI Training Policy (pcgamer.com) 43
			
		 	
				"I burned my Etsy shop to the ground this week," illustrator Aaron Millard posted on Instagram:
 8 years, 11,200 sales, 3k+ reviews, hundreds in a customer base. Deleted.
Etsy decided that selling on their platform now means letting them train AI on our artwork AND resell that data to third parties, with no way to opt out (in Canada, anyways)...
 
Etsy's new Terms of Use — going into effect December 15 — include this language in their section about "Your Content":
You also recognize our legitimate interest in using it... This also includes the right for us and our third party partners and vendors to use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies, including to improve the Services and/or help keep them safe, subject to any applicable opt-out rights described in our Privacy Policy.  
"My work took years to learn and create," illustrator Millard wrote on Instagram. "I won't let it be stolen. It's not free fuel for an AI slop business model."
Following Etsy's announcement "artists are shutting down their shops in droves," writes Cartoon Brew, "and posting illustrated goodbye notes to tell customers where to find them next."
Ironically, just weeks ago, Etsy announced tighter rules on misleading AI product photos and bot-generated listings. The marketplace still allows sellers to list work generated from their own prompts, as long as they disclose the use of AI to buyers.
Etsy says it uses sellers' content to spot fraud and help shoppers find products, and that it doesn't train models designed to copy artists' work. That said, the vague terms leave open just how its partners and vendors might use that same content...
The artists posting their goodbyes have decided it's worth walking away from that revenue source to keep their work from being used to train AI.
 
"In the wake of that reaction, Etsy vice president of customer operations James Ossman posted a separate update," writes PC Gamer, "saying it's not really like that at all... [T]hat 'we do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity.'"
"... we're enabling actions like translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work," Ossman wrote. "We also use your content to develop tools that make running your shop easier, like listing optimization tools or stats summaries that help you better understand your shop's performance. As always, your needs and feedback help guide how we build and improve these tools."
As for providing third-party access to that content, Ossman said that too is for "services and tools that can help you run your business," and promised that "when we partner with third parties, we do so thoughtfully to help protect your content and data."
That hasn't satisfied everyone. Ossman's commitment doesn't exist within the actual terms of service, which as seen above states only that Etsy and partners can "use Your Content to develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." Ossman also noted in his update that the terms "prohibit scraping Etsy or unauthorized use of content from Etsy to train AI models," but that (as far as I can tell) applies to Etsy users and unauthorized third-parties, not Etsy itself or those it licenses...
Others also complain that AI training should be opt-in rather than on by default — and worse, there's apparently no opt-out option available at all, so users who are opposed to having their work used for AI training for any reason are out of luck.
Ironically, the blowup over Etsy's embrace of AI training comes just weeks after it earned plaudits for banning AI-generated recipes and patterns, a move Ossman said was necessary to establish "trust" in the platform.

articles.title: Jensen Huang scheduled to testify next week in Senate following reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to a notice on the committee’s website.
The development comes just hours after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive, less than two weeks following his resignation after it was revealed that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government of working as a Chinese spy.
The Senate Banking Committee has jurisdiction over export control policies that are designed to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies, such as chips capable of powering AI models, from falling into the hands of foreign governments and militaries.
The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy and his potential involvement in chip-smuggling operations.
It’s worth noting that before his reinstatement as CEO, Huang had already agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee on December 1.

articles.title: GrapheneOS Accuses Google of Kneecapping Its Android Partners Using Pixel Exclusives
articles.body:
GrapheneOS Accuses Google of Kneecapping Its Android Partners Using Pixel Exclusives (itsfoss.com) 23
			
		 	
				Last year Slashed reported that the privacy- and security-focused Android fork GrapheneOS was "partnering with a major Android OEM to bring its hardened, de-Googled OS to Snapdragon-powered flagship phones." 
And early this November Motorola announced their upcoming high end Signature 27 phone would include official support for GrapheneOS as an OS option, the first Motorola device supporting GrapheneOS.
But the nonprofit GrapheneOS project has a new problem, reports the blog It's FOSS :
GrapheneOS has accused Google of leaning on phone makers to keep away from the project. The claim came in a thread on X [Thursday], where the project says makers were questioned about working with it, then threatened over their Google app licensing.... The project says Google is working against GrapheneOS itself and expects it to go further. It sees Pixel bootloaders being locked down eventually and Play Integrity, an API it calls illegal, being pushed harder. And if that were to happen, Android forks would struggle to survive under that.  
GrapheneOS believes some of Google's conduct breaks US criminal law and that antitrust violations can put individuals in prison. It wants to talk to the [U.S.] Department of Justice and says earlier cases against Google left its most serious violations largely untouched. Supporters are being asked for introductions to prosecutors and regulators, with assurances that the project has the necessary resources to carry on no matter what happens.  
GrapheneOS says more Android features and updates now stay Pixel only, leaving other hardware partners behind.

articles.title: GTA VI’s pretentious puzzler makes indie developers feel ‘part of larger culture’
articles.body:
One of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux. It’s a moody, black-and-white title with obtuse puzzles and a main character that constantly narrates to himself with dramatic language. Its credits attribute pretty much everything to a developer named Johannes Zuch. It’s generated a lot of discussion for seemingly mocking games like Jonathan Blow’s The Witness or The Chinese Room’s Dear Esther. It’s also a game that only exists inside of Grand Theft Auto VI.
GTA VI’s pretentious puzzler makes indie developers feel ‘part of larger culture’
Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and big-budget blockbusters.
Developer Rockstar Games has stuffed a lot of satirical media inside of GTA VI, including TV shows you can watch, books you can read, and radio shows you can listen to. It’s all in service of making the world feel like a funhouse-mirror version of our current reality — Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis plays a right-wing radio host, for example. There are more games you can play inside GTA VI in addition to Tenebrae Lux, including a zombie-themed roguelike. But Tenebrae Lux, which you have to see as part of GTA VI’s main story, is the one that has struck a chord, including with indie developers like Sam Barlow and Robert Yang.
“I have to admit it’s kind of funny for the biggest blockbuster game of all time to go after arthouse indie,” Yang tells The Verge, noting that it’s “like a fighter jet getting obsessed with an ant, petty in a funny way.” (Given that GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day, the gulf between Rockstar and indie game studios that are struggling to get by is vast.)
But Yang suggested that Rockstar developers are probably well versed in the types of games they’re lampooning in GTA VI. “I don’t think gamers understand how much indie experimental stuff any decent AAA dev plays,” Yang said, pointing out that Rockstar’s environmental artists and level designers “all probably love Dear Esther,” the influential first-person game that helped popularize the “walking sim” concept when it launched in 2012.
“I was mostly taken with what it meant that the millions of people playing the game were having to sit down and play through an extended gag about indie games,” Barlow tells The Verge. “That made me feel like we were part of larger culture.” He added that he hopes some of these players might “seek out what these arty indie games might be.”
Rockstar is self-aware enough to use its video games to poke fun at the medium itself. As part of a long conversation between protagonist Jason Duval and his friend Cal Hampton before they start playing Tenebrae Lux, Cal hypes the game by saying that none of it is “just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking.” Initially, you only play Tenebrae Lux for a few minutes, which is enough time to get stumped on the initial puzzles, before the game cuts back to Jason being bored. “Got anything else, a little less, uh… y’know?” he asks. They play the zombie game, titled Street Trash 3 Dezombifier, right after. (You can go back and play the entirety of Tenebrae Lux later if you want.)
Barlow said that the cut “felt very true to the character and story. I gather there is more to the game, but it felt natural to me to hit a wall with the pretentious puzzle design and then move on!”
Yang also pointed out that from a design perspective, GTA VI has more in common with Tenebrae Lux than Street Trash 3 Dezombifier. GTA VI is “basically a walking sim where you walk around Florida and listen to people talk,” Yang said. “What’s the difference? Well, just like a billion dollars I guess.”

articles.title: Amazon is taking orders for the Moto Tag 3 before it’s even been announced
articles.body:
Motorola’s unannounced Moto Tag 3 has been listed for sale online, just five months after the Moto Tag 2 went on sale in the US, and before any official announcement of a follow-up. The listing on Amazon UK was spotted by X user @matteventu, and shows the tracker in a “Pantone Lucent White” color option, with a price of £24.96 (about $33) and a 1-4 month shipping estimate.
Amazon is taking orders for the Moto Tag 3 before it’s even been announced
The Amazon UK listing for Motorola’s new tracking tag has been live since Friday.
A second image shared by leaker Evan Blass also shows a vibrant purple version of the new tracking tag, which is described as “Pantone Indigo Blue” on a separate Amazon Italy listing. Both are new color options, with the Moto Tag 2 only currently available in orange or a grey-ish beige. While the Moto Tag 3 name suggests this is a follow-up to the Moto Tag 2, there don’t appear to be any major hardware differences between the two trackers.
Both use a replaceable CR2032 battery, claim to provide more than 500 days of battery life, and support UWB in Android Find Hub, among other similarities. The XT2561-1 model number seen on the back of the Moto Tag 3 images also matches that of the Moto Tag 2. That could mean that the Moto Tag 3 name is an error and these are just new color options for the Tag 2.
We’ve asked Motorola for clarification and will update if we hear back.

articles.title: How should an LLM see a computer?
articles.body:
Introduction
Claude Code and Codex can both use your computer. Under the hood they work in a similar manner: both can give the model a screenshot and an accessibility tree, a text description of every button on screen, and let it click by position or by naming an element.
The text version of the screen was built decades ago, for people who couldn’t see it. In 1984, two IBM mathematicians, Jim Thatcher and his former thesis adviser, Jesse Wright, who was blind, started a side project to read the PC’s screen out loud. When GUIs turned the screen into pixels, apps had to start describing themselves instead. Microsoft shipped Active Accessibility in 1997, Sun started AT-SPI for Linux in 2001, and Apple added its Accessibility API in 2002.
This text has been useful for agents too. On the 2024 OSWorld benchmark, models looking only at screenshots completed about one task in twenty, while most models reading the screen as text did better.
How do those results hold up with stronger models? We tested screenshots on their own and with the accessibility tree on seven models, and used the results to decide how our QA agent, TREX, should see the screen.
What's so hard about clicking a button?
A person clicks a button by moving the mouse to it. A model, on the other hand, looks at a screenshot and has to write the coordinates out as text (e.g., ‘x=523, y=217’) before clicking on it. Getting these numbers off by a few pixels can mean it clicks the wrong thing.
The same button sits at different coordinates on different screen and window sizes, so the guesses get worse when the resolution changes.
Also, the model’s vision works against it as it doesn’t see a screenshot pixel by pixel. The image is initially shrunk to fit the model's size limit, then cut into tiny squares, each dozens of pixels wide. But a click still has to land on one exact pixel.
Small targets are hard. On ScreenSpot-Pro, a 2025 benchmark with tiny targets on high resolution screens, the best model at release hit the right target only 18.9% of the time. Anthropic’s own docs warn that Claude “might make mistakes or hallucinate when outputting specific coordinates.”
When OSWorld came out in 2024, human testers were able to complete 72% of its tasks, and the best model about 12%. The authors found that models struggled with two things: turning ‘click Save’ into the right point on the screen, and knowing how to operate the software.
The first problem has a seemingly obvious fix. The accessibility tree already reveals each button's location, so the model doesn't have to go through the trouble of finding pixels. Go one step further, and the model doesn’t even need coordinates; it can pick a button by ID and let the harness click it. To test this, we built three setups, each building upon the last:
- Screenshots alone
- Adding an accessibility tree (clicking by coordinates)
- Adding clicks by element IDs
Every setup used the same agent on 172 OSWorld tasks, with one attempt per task, a 50-step limit and low reasoning effort, scored by OSWorld’s own graders.
Starting with screenshots
The model runs in a loop where it first sees a screenshot and past actions, picks an action (click coordinates, type or press keys), and then looks at the changes. It’s the simplest way to give a model a computer, and the one most agents start with. OSWorld’s baseline agent supports it, and Anthropic described its first computer use model as looking at screenshots and counting how many pixels to move the cursor.
We ran the same screenshot agent across seven OpenAI models:
On our 172 tasks, GPT-4.1 scored a mere 5.4% with screenshots alone, while the more recent GPT-6.1 Sol scored 83.8%. On the much harder OSWorld 2.0 offline set, OpenAI reports a score of 71.4% for GPT-6.1 Sol at maximum reasoning effort. The gap between the two models raised questions: do stronger models even need the tree, and can it help weaker ones catch up?
Adding the accessibility tree
Here, the model sees the screenshot with an accessibility tree beside it. We were interested in the tree because it can just tell the model what’s there, like a button labeled “Save” and where it sits. The model still clicks by coordinates here. The tree lists each element's position and dimensions in pixels, so the model can work out where to click after doing the math. With the clicking kept constant, the only thing that changed was what the model saw.
OSWorld runs on Linux, so our agents read AT-SPI. Each app's toolkit, such as GTK or Qt, describes its widgets, and a small bridge passes those descriptions on to any program that asks for them, without any permission prompt. While testing, we realized that GIMP was missing from the tree entirely until we added back an environment variable set at login.
In our evals, trees helped every model that struggled with screenshots. GPT-5.2 went from 15.8% with screenshots alone to 36.2% with the tree added, and GPT-4.1 from 5.4% to 20.6%. On the other hand, strong models barely budged. GPT-6.1 Sol scored 82.7% with the tree, slightly worse than with screenshots alone (83.8%) and none of the three strongest models changed by a statistically significant amount.
Clicking by ID
Next, we gave each element in the tree an ID. The model can simply name the element it wants and the harness clicks it. This bypasses the problem of clicking the exact pixel.
For weaker models, ID clicks boosted performance on top of the tree. GPT-5.2 went from 36.2% with the tree + coordinates to 52.8% when it clicked by ID, and GPT-4.1 from 20.6% to 29.3%. Put together, the tree and ID clicks more than tripled GPT-5.2’s score with screenshots alone (15.8%).
Again, this experiment didn't do much for the strongest models. GPT-6.1 Sol scored 82.7% clicking by coordinates and 82.1% clicking by ID.
It depends on the model
For the three strongest models, neither step made a difference. Across both steps, the four weaker models gained 9 to 37 points with the tree and ID clicks, more than doubling their scores in three of four cases. If you’re building on weaker models, the tree is still worth adding.
Some apps publish no tree at all. A canvas app like Figma publishes its toolbar buttons, but the canvas itself is just pixels, and a game like Doom is pixels from top to bottom. Even in apps with a good tree, some bugs only show on screen, like text that overflows its box. The screenshot covers all of these.
TREX Computer Use
Code review catches bugs in the diff. Some bugs only exist when the software is running: a button that can’t be clicked, a label that runs off the edge of the window. Until now, catching those took a person opening the app and simulating the user flow. By writing more code and touching more of the UI than any team can check by hand, coding agents have made it hard for programmers to keep up.
That’s why we built computer use into TREX. It runs the changes in your pull request on an actual desktop and uses the app the way a person would, so you can see that the feature you asked for is the one that got built.
How TREX sees the screen came out of these experiments. It runs on the best models and relies on the screenshot at every step. It uses the accessibility tree to click by ID when it can, and coordinates when the tree doesn't have the element, like a canvas or a game.
How a model should see the screen depends on the model, so we'll rerun these experiments each time a new one comes out and update TREX when the answer changes.
When something breaks on screen, TREX catches it, and shows you what happened.
Try TREX on your next pull request.
