articles.title: Building a wireless network adapter for the Super Nintendo
articles.body:
00 Why?
I always come back to the Super Nintendo (SNES). It was my first console and it’s still my most potent source of nostalgia. It inspired my early interest in electronics as a teenager, designing circuits for mods and flash carts that I hoped to build one day. I followed the launch of Hackaday, Adafruit, and the progress of bunnie Huang’s Chumby and knew exactly what I wanted to do.
I dropped out of my final years of high school to study hands-on electronics at college, and continued on to university. Then, finally equipped with those skills I’d aspired to, I went off-track and spent the next fifteen years working in data, ML and software. A lot has changed in that time but I’m back now, picking up exactly where I left off.
The Super Network Adapter is an exercise in ‘16-bit futurism’, it aims to be a faithful peripheral to the original SNES hardware and what we imagined the future might be back then: a wireless link to the net, sync’ing saves across devices and an uplink to AI.
01 Prototyping
The SNES never had a dedicated network port. The closest it came was the Satellaview, a modem peripheral connected to a hidden expansion port that could receive game broadcasts via satellite. There was also the XBAND, a modem that plugged into the cartridge slot and supported pass-through patching of specific games for online play. Reproducing the hardware of either of these today would be challenging, however most peripherals for the SNES took a much simpler route, they used one of the controller ports.
Controller Serial Link
      The SNES controller ports are small synchronous serial buses that a game can control, setting and reading individual lines and driving the clock. These ports have seven lines but in a typical controller cable, only five tend to be present, with the wires for D1 and IOBit left out. To make sourcing parts for this project easier, my design also only relies on the remaining five wires.
      
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
 │ ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────────╮ │
 │ │  ●       ●       ●       ●   │  │   ●       ●       ●   │ │
 │ └──────────────────────────────┘  └───────────────────────╯ │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
      1       2       3       4          5       6       7
      5v     CLK    Latch     D0         D1    IOBit    GND
    
    First I needed a protocol for talking over this serial link, which I iterated with Mesen and a virtual network adapter written in Lua simulating the controller port link. This protocol has the SNES writing to the Latch line and reading from the adapter on D0, one bit at a time (‘bit-banging’). Even with some optimisation (unrolling loops and ignoring mid-stream replies) this approach tops out at about 30 KB/s, but that’s enough for the ’90s.
    
Breadboard Version
The first physical prototype was built using a Pico 2 W dev board. The additional circuitry needed was very simple, just some pull-up resistors for CLK and Latch. The board’s RP2350A can handle the console’s 5v logic on its pins directly, and it has two cores: one can maintain the console link, while the other maintains the Wi-Fi network link, without juggling interrupts.
Controller port pinout
The prototype runs from USB, with the console’s 5v only feeding the pull-ups. I did not connect the SNES 5v to the Pico’s VBUS or VSYS while USB is plugged in. The Pico was powered on before the console so the RP2350’s pins were ready to handle 5v. The PCB design later can run on either supply.
02 Save sync
Adding Cloud Save or ‘Save Sync’ seemed the most practical use for a Wi-Fi connection. I often go back to the SNES and start a new game, but if I could continue playing that save file in RetroArch on my phone and then back to the SNES, it would fit into my life much more easily.
      Game save data is stored in battery-backed SRAM and in order for a game to send that through my adapter, I needed some of my own code to run. I already have a programmable flash cart for the SNES, so I wrote a utility to patch ROMs and inject this ‘save sync’ code into the reset vector. At power-on and whenever the console is reset, it syncs the save data through the adapter to a WebDAV server as saves/<core>/<name>.srm (the same path RetroArch uses) so the console save can be continued on the phone, and vice versa.
    
Joining Wi-Fi
First though, the adapter needs to join the local Wi-Fi network. I wanted an era-appropriate UI that can be run from a setup ROM (fig.2), which has you pick a network and type its password with an on-screen keyboard, one letter at a time. That felt most ‘authentic’ but I also made a second iteration that shows the typical QR code on the TV for setup via mobile phone.
The second version has the adapter set up a temporary network. Scanning the QR code with a phone joins the network and it then does the usual captive portal flow to open the adapter’s setup page, where the network and WebDAV auth details can be input in a much more user-friendly way.
Pushing and Pulling Saves
An important detail to get right was checking whether the save on the cartridge was newest, or whether to download a newer one from WebDAV. RetroArch keeps a manifest file with a hash of every save, so the adapter updates that too, comparing hashes to decide whether the cartridge or the server has the newest save. If both sides have changed, nothing is overwritten and the cartridge’s save goes to a conflicts folder to play it safe.
SRAM saves are small but this sync still has to run whenever a game starts, potentially introducing a delay. To avoid this, the save is split into chunks that each have their own checksum, so only the chunks that have changed are sent over the controller port. In practice this makes the save sync delay imperceptible, and only when an existing save is pulled by the SNES for the first time is there a 1-2s load screen.
03 AI dialogue
Naturally in 2026, an internet connection also means a connection to LLMs. The dialogue in SNES-era games tends to be fixed and unresponsive. In A Link to the Past, the villagers don’t react when you smash their pots (unlike in subsequent Zelda games). With the network adapter though, we can hook the game’s dialogue text renderer to swap out the original text for an in-character line generated by an LLM.
In order to prompt for dialogue, the LLM needs to be passed the game context, such as the character being interacted with and recent events. Since Link to the Past has been fully disassembled, it was possible to patch it to accumulate this state in RAM and push it out over the controller serial to the adapter and on to an LLM (via a proxy I ran on a local machine that holds the API key).
I tried a few different models and settled on Claude Opus 5.5, as cheaper models would break character or leak spoilers despite being prompted not to. I used LLM as a Judge evals to measure the proportion of responses that fit the context - Haiku scored 66%, Sonnet 90% and Opus 98%. The challenge was the time to first token of the LLM, for Haiku it was about 0.8 s but for Opus it averaged 2.2 s.
To avoid game-breaking delays from the LLM response times, I switched to speculatively generating the dialogue when Link approaches an NPC, storing the responses in a cache and invalidating them as the context updates. The delay from using a larger model was hidden and most NPC interactions had the response ready. This is a great way to burn tokens so probably not something to do for the full game duration!
04 Hardware
When designing the PCB version of the adapter (fig.0) I replicated the same architecture as the prototype, an RP2350A microcontroller that handles the 5v lines and maintains the serial link, with an ESP32-C3 Wi-Fi coprocessor that handles the Wi-Fi connection. These communicate with each other over UART, allowing each link to be maintained by a dedicated core.
┌─────────┐ port 2 ┌─────────┐ uart ┌──────────┐ wi-fi ┌────────┐
│ SNES    │──────▸ │ RP2350A │────▸ │ ESP32-C3 │~~~~~▸ │ cloud  │
│ 65816   │◂────── │ PIO     │◂──── │ TCP/TLS  │◂~~~~~ │ WebDAV │
└─────────┘        └─────────┘      └──────────┘       └────────┘
  3.58 MHz           150 MHz          160 MHz
      A PIO state machine on the RP2350 watches clock and latch, queueing the data and filtering out glitches shorter than 100 ns. This frees up the cores to prepare data to be sent over D0 while also talking to the C3.
    
The USB socket was included not just for flashing the board but also to support debugging it while it is powered from the SNES. This means the board needs to safely support taking a 5v supply from either the controller port or USB, and avoid backfeeding if both are connected. This is done with a LM66200 dual ideal diode. Supply can be taken from either source and we avoid the voltage drop that would come with using actual diodes. I’d seen some brownouts in tests on the breadboard, so designed the PCB with plenty of headroom for the LDO regulator even if the supply rail sags on a Wi-Fi burst.
While prototyping I also had issues when using series resistors on the link lines. This may be related to erratum RP2350-E9 in the A2 revision (stepping) of the RP2350A on my Pico 2 W. In the assembled PCB order I switched these to 0 Ω links, as they’re just for protection and I wasn’t sure which stepping the PCB would be assembled with. The boards turned out to have the fixed A4 stepping, so real resistors can go in next time.
05 Enclosure
The case is just a tray and a lid that sandwich the PCB, though I did want it to nod toward an era-appropriate design language. It was generated in code (build123d) using the PCB’s STEP files from KiCad, so that the design could be tested within a single 3D model.
The two halves join around the cable and the USB socket, and there are M2 pillars that align with the drilled holes in the PCB to hold everything together.
Since the PCB has a status LED, this design has a light pipe that channels that light up to become the dot of the etched Wi-Fi icon. It’s not the prettiest of designs, but I thought that was cute.
I’ve ordered a batch of these enclosures to be 3D printed and will update with actual photos once they arrive and the adapter is fully assembled. I’m also considering how to fabricate a single assembly that can insert directly into the controller port. Reach out at [email protected] if you’re interested!
06 Build log
- 65816 toolchain, headless emulator tests
- Breadboard link to port 2 working
- First save uploaded from the console
- PCB designed and ordered from JLCPCB
- PCBs arrive and work perfectly!
- Ordered 3D printed enclosures
- Awaiting delivery of enclosures

articles.title: Win4wine – Run Windows Shell as the Linux Desktop on Wine
articles.body:
Linux のデスクトップを、Windows XP のシェルで。
日本語 · English
Important
個人の実験的なプロジェクトです。 日常の作業環境として使えるほど完成してはいません。 動作を確かめているのは、新しくインストールした Debian 13 に導入スクリプトで入れた場合だけです。 すでに使っている環境（ほかのデスクトップ環境やディスプレイマネージャが入っているものなど）への導入は試していません。 試すときは、仮想マシンや試験用のマシンをおすすめします。
Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを当てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェルとして動かすプロジェクトです。
タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。
Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。
XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル（Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも 試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、導入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（docs/reactos.md）。
Windows 7 の ISO があれば、Windows 7 のシェル（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（docs/windows7.md）。
- XP のシェル: Luna（またはクラシック）のタスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、マイ コンピュータ、フォルダウィンドウ。
- Linux アプリとの統合: Linux のウィンドウに XP の枠が付き、タスクバー、Alt+Tab、最小化・最大化が XP と同じように動きます。 Linux のアプリは「すべてのプログラム」に並びます。
- 通知領域: Linux のトレイアイコン（StatusNotifierItem と XEmbed）が XP の通知領域に出ます。 XP 自身のネットワーク・バッテリー・音量のアイコンと、そのフライアウト（音量、電源メーター、ワイヤレス ネットワーク接続の状態）も 出ます。NetworkManager と PipeWire / PulseAudio の状態から作ります（AshesTom さんのフォークの XP Explorer から）。 ワイヤレス ネットワークの一覧から、初めてのネットワークにも XP のネットワーク キーの画面で接続できます。メニューや画面の文字は ISO の XP のファイルから読みます。
- XP Explorer からの追加: フォルダの左のタスク ペイン、画面のプロパティ（Windows XP とクラシックのテーマ、スタイルと配色。
配色は ISO の HIVEDEF.INF と themeui.dll から作ります）、画像の縮小版とプレビュー、XP のサウンド（起動、ログオン、ログオフも）、
ネットワーク接続、Internet Explorer 6、Windows Media Player 9、スタートメニューの左の列（インターネット、電子メール、
よく使うプログラム）。どれもお手元の ISO のファイルで動きます（prefix/extras.py）。
- キーボードの配列: 最初は Linux のシステムの配列（localectl）です。コントロール パネルの「地域と言語のオプション」→
「言語」→「詳細」（XP 自身のもの）で入力言語を足したり既定を変えたりすると、セッションの配列（Wayland では labwc、
X11 では setxkbmap）がすぐに従います。2 つ以上なら XP と同じ左 Alt+Shift で切り替わります（session/keyboard.py）。
- 日本語入力: fcitx5 + Mozc です。Ctrl+Space（または全角/半角）で切り替えます。GTK、Qt、Wine のアプリで使えます。
- 日本語版と英語版の XP: どちらの ISO でも動きます。言語は ISO から自動で判断し、字体（英語版は Tahoma など）、 ロケール、ようこそ画面をその XP に合わせます（英語版では日本語入力は設定しません）。
- Windows のアプリ: WoW64 の Wine 11.0 で、32bit と 64bit のアプリが動きます。端末で wine setup.exe と打つと、
インストーラーが作るショートカットは XP のスタートメニューに入ります。
- XP のようこそ画面: LightDM の greeter として、XP のようこそ画面とログオフの画面を出せます（任意）。 シェルが起動するまでは XP と同じ大きな「ようこそ」の画面を出します。
- XP のキー操作: Windows キー、Ctrl+Esc、Win+R、Win+E が使えます。
- クイック起動: タスクバーの右クリック →「ツール バー」→「クイック起動」で出せます（XP と ReactOS。Windows 7 は実機と同じく 「新規ツール バー」でクイック起動のフォルダを選びます）。スタートメニューから Linux のアプリのショートカットも置けます。 「デスクトップの表示」も実機と同じく、もう一度押すと窓が元に戻ります。
- 画面の拡大（DPI）: XP と同じ「DPI 設定」で、文字や部品を大きくできます（96・120・144 など）。
- 落ちても戻れる: XP のシェルが繰り返し落ちると、Wine 標準の explorer と xterm に切り替わります。
- Wayland のセッション（任意・X11 のセッション以上に実験的）: X11 のウィンドウマネージャーの代わりに、パッチを当てた labwc で 動かすセッションです（XP、ReactOS、Windows 7 のシェル）。モニターごとの倍率や 125%・150% などの倍率が使え、シェルはぼけずに描かれます。 Wayland のアプリにもシェルの枠が付きます。作ったばかりで、確かめた範囲は X11 のセッションより狭く、既知の制限もあります（docs/wayland.md）。 ふだん試すなら X11 のセッションをおすすめします。
- ReactOS のシェル（任意）: XP の ISO の代わりに ReactOS 0.4.16 の explorer で動かすセッションです。日本語と英語に対応します。 XP のシェルと並べて入れられます。
- Windows 7 のシェル（任意・実験的）: Windows 7 SP1 x64 の explorer で動かすセッションです（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目。 Aero のガラスはまだありません）。スタートメニュー、タスクバー、通知領域、フォルダの窓が動き、Linux のアプリもアプリごとに タスクバーにまとまります。確かめたのは日本語版と、その文字を英語の言語パックのものに入れ替えた英語版です。
- Windows XP Professional SP3（x86）の ISO（日本語版か英語版）をご自身で用意してください。
- 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に、ログインして使う利用者として入り、次を実行します。
git clone https://github.com/mikuta0407/win4wine.git ~/win4wine
cd ~/win4wine
scripts/setup.sh --media /path/to/WindowsXPSP3.iso --greeter
- 再起動すると、XP のようこそ画面からそのまま XP のシェルに入ります。
XP の ISO が無いときは、ReactOS のシェルで試せます（ISO は要りません）。
scripts/setup.sh --shell reactos --lang ja   # 英語なら --lang en
ログイン画面でセッション「ReactOS Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。
Windows 7 のシェル（実験的）は、Windows 7 SP1 x64 の ISO から作ります。
scripts/setup.sh --shell win7 --media /path/to/Windows7SP1x64.iso
ログイン画面でセッション「Windows 7 Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。
詳しい手順とオプションは 🔗 導入手順（INSTALL.md） にあります。Wine をソースからビルドするので、4 コアで 1 時間半ほどかかります。 テーマ（XP のクラシックなど）と文字の大きさは、後から変えられます（見た目と文字の大きさを変える）。
Warning
- Windows XP（と Windows 7）の ISO はご自身で入手してください。 このリポジトリにも導入スクリプトにも、Microsoft のファイルを 取得する処理はありません。ISO と取り出したファイルの扱いは、Microsoft の使用許諾に従ってください。
- 利用は自己責任でお願いします。 データの損失や不具合について、作者は責任を負いません。
- Microsoft とも Wine プロジェクトとも関係のない、非公式のプロジェクトです。
- 確かめているのは日本語版と英語版の XP SP3（x86）だけです。ほかの言語の XP も英語版と同じ設定で入れるので動くかもしれませんが、
一切試していません（setup.sh は警告を出して続けます）。
LightDM ─ XP のようこそ画面 (greeter/)
   └─ XP Shell セッション (session/supervisor.py)
        ├─ Wine 11.0 + 151 本のパッチ (wine/patches/)
        │    └─ XP の explorer.exe, shell32.dll, …（ISO から取り出したもの。ReactOS や Windows 7 のシェルではそれらのもの）
        ├─ bridge-wm: X11 のウィンドウマネージャー + Win32 の代理ウィンドウ (bridge-wm/)
        │    （Wayland のセッションでは、ウィンドウマネージャーの代わりにパッチを当てた labwc。wayland/）
        └─ fcitx5 + Mozc, トレイの仲介 (bridge-wm/tray.py)
仕組みや設計の詳しい説明は docs/ にまとめています。
- loss32: Wine の上の Win32 のソフトウェアだけでデスクトップを作る Linux ディストリビューションの計画です。 ReactOS の部品も使います。win4wine が XP 本物のシェルを Debian の上で動かすのに対し、loss32 は自由なソフトウェアだけで作ります。
- Windows 由来のバイナリには手を加えません。違いは Wine とその周辺で吸収します。
- Microsoft のバイナリを逆アセンブルしません。挙動は公開 API と、実際の XP の上で動かす自作のプローブで調べています。
- Microsoft のファイル、取り出したもの、Wine の prefix は、Git 管理外の localres/ と .local/ にだけ置きます。
- AshesTom さん（フォーク）: XP の画面のプロパティ、
サウンド、キーボードの配列、通知領域の XP のアイコン、スタートメニューの左の列、Internet Explorer 6 と Windows Media Player 9、
起動中のようこそ画面、タイトルバーのアニメーションと小さいアイコン、Arch Linux への対応、xp.sh など。
LGPL-2.1-or-later（Wine と同じ）です。対象はこのリポジトリのコードとパッチだけです。
ただし wayland/patches/labwc/ は labwc と同じ GPL-2.0-only、wayland/patches/wlroots/ は wlroots と同じ MIT です。
Windows XP と Windows 7 のファイルと、スクリーンショットに写っている XP と Windows 7 の画面の著作権は Microsoft にあります。
ReactOS のシェルで使う ReactOS のファイルは、ReactOS のライセンス（GPL-2.0-or-later、DLL の多くは LGPL-2.1-or-later）に従います。

日本語 · English
Important
個人の実験的なプロジェクトです。 日常の作業環境として使えるほど完成してはいません。 動作を確かめているのは、新しくインストールした Debian 13 に導入スクリプトで入れた場合だけです。 すでに使っている環境（ほかのデスクトップ環境やディスプレイマネージャが入っているものなど）への導入は試していません。 試すときは、仮想マシンや試験用のマシンをおすすめします。
Windows XP の explorer.exe を、パッチを当てた Wine の上で Linux のデスクトップシェルとして動かすプロジェクトです。
タスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、フォルダウィンドウは XP 本物のものです。Linux のアプリも、XP の枠とタスクバーで扱えます。
Microsoft のファイルは同梱していません。お手元の XP の ISO から、必要なファイルだけを取り出して使います。
XP の ISO が無い方は、XP のシェルの代わりに ReactOS のシェル（Windows 2000 風のクラシックの見た目）でも 試せます。ReactOS は自由なソフトウェアなので、導入スクリプトが公式のリリースから取得します（docs/reactos.md）。
Windows 7 の ISO があれば、Windows 7 のシェル（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目）でも試せます。まだ実験的な試作です（docs/windows7.md）。
- XP のシェル: Luna（またはクラシック）のタスクバー、スタートメニュー、デスクトップ、マイ コンピュータ、フォルダウィンドウ。
- Linux アプリとの統合: Linux のウィンドウに XP の枠が付き、タスクバー、Alt+Tab、最小化・最大化が XP と同じように動きます。 Linux のアプリは「すべてのプログラム」に並びます。
- 通知領域: Linux のトレイアイコン（StatusNotifierItem と XEmbed）が XP の通知領域に出ます。 XP 自身のネットワーク・バッテリー・音量のアイコンと、そのフライアウト（音量、電源メーター、ワイヤレス ネットワーク接続の状態）も 出ます。NetworkManager と PipeWire / PulseAudio の状態から作ります（AshesTom さんのフォークの XP Explorer から）。 ワイヤレス ネットワークの一覧から、初めてのネットワークにも XP のネットワーク キーの画面で接続できます。メニューや画面の文字は ISO の XP のファイルから読みます。
- XP Explorer からの追加: フォルダの左のタスク ペイン、画面のプロパティ（Windows XP とクラシックのテーマ、スタイルと配色。
配色は ISO の HIVEDEF.INF と themeui.dll から作ります）、画像の縮小版とプレビュー、XP のサウンド（起動、ログオン、ログオフも）、
ネットワーク接続、Internet Explorer 6、Windows Media Player 9、スタートメニューの左の列（インターネット、電子メール、
よく使うプログラム）。どれもお手元の ISO のファイルで動きます（prefix/extras.py）。
- キーボードの配列: 最初は Linux のシステムの配列（localectl）です。コントロール パネルの「地域と言語のオプション」→
「言語」→「詳細」（XP 自身のもの）で入力言語を足したり既定を変えたりすると、セッションの配列（Wayland では labwc、
X11 では setxkbmap）がすぐに従います。2 つ以上なら XP と同じ左 Alt+Shift で切り替わります（session/keyboard.py）。
- 日本語入力: fcitx5 + Mozc です。Ctrl+Space（または全角/半角）で切り替えます。GTK、Qt、Wine のアプリで使えます。
- 日本語版と英語版の XP: どちらの ISO でも動きます。言語は ISO から自動で判断し、字体（英語版は Tahoma など）、 ロケール、ようこそ画面をその XP に合わせます（英語版では日本語入力は設定しません）。
- Windows のアプリ: WoW64 の Wine 11.0 で、32bit と 64bit のアプリが動きます。端末で wine setup.exe と打つと、
インストーラーが作るショートカットは XP のスタートメニューに入ります。
- XP のようこそ画面: LightDM の greeter として、XP のようこそ画面とログオフの画面を出せます（任意）。 シェルが起動するまでは XP と同じ大きな「ようこそ」の画面を出します。
- XP のキー操作: Windows キー、Ctrl+Esc、Win+R、Win+E が使えます。
- クイック起動: タスクバーの右クリック →「ツール バー」→「クイック起動」で出せます（XP と ReactOS。Windows 7 は実機と同じく 「新規ツール バー」でクイック起動のフォルダを選びます）。スタートメニューから Linux のアプリのショートカットも置けます。 「デスクトップの表示」も実機と同じく、もう一度押すと窓が元に戻ります。
- 画面の拡大（DPI）: XP と同じ「DPI 設定」で、文字や部品を大きくできます（96・120・144 など）。
- 落ちても戻れる: XP のシェルが繰り返し落ちると、Wine 標準の explorer と xterm に切り替わります。
- Wayland のセッション（任意・X11 のセッション以上に実験的）: X11 のウィンドウマネージャーの代わりに、パッチを当てた labwc で 動かすセッションです（XP、ReactOS、Windows 7 のシェル）。モニターごとの倍率や 125%・150% などの倍率が使え、シェルはぼけずに描かれます。 Wayland のアプリにもシェルの枠が付きます。作ったばかりで、確かめた範囲は X11 のセッションより狭く、既知の制限もあります（docs/wayland.md）。 ふだん試すなら X11 のセッションをおすすめします。
- ReactOS のシェル（任意）: XP の ISO の代わりに ReactOS 0.4.16 の explorer で動かすセッションです。日本語と英語に対応します。 XP のシェルと並べて入れられます。
- Windows 7 のシェル（任意・実験的）: Windows 7 SP1 x64 の explorer で動かすセッションです（Windows 7 ベーシックの見た目。 Aero のガラスはまだありません）。スタートメニュー、タスクバー、通知領域、フォルダの窓が動き、Linux のアプリもアプリごとに タスクバーにまとまります。確かめたのは日本語版と、その文字を英語の言語パックのものに入れ替えた英語版です。
- Windows XP Professional SP3（x86）の ISO（日本語版か英語版）をご自身で用意してください。
- 新しくインストールした Debian 13 に、ログインして使う利用者として入り、次を実行します。
git clone https://github.com/mikuta0407/win4wine.git ~/win4wine
cd ~/win4wine
scripts/setup.sh --media /path/to/WindowsXPSP3.iso --greeter
- 再起動すると、XP のようこそ画面からそのまま XP のシェルに入ります。
XP の ISO が無いときは、ReactOS のシェルで試せます（ISO は要りません）。
scripts/setup.sh --shell reactos --lang ja   # 英語なら --lang en
ログイン画面でセッション「ReactOS Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。
Windows 7 のシェル（実験的）は、Windows 7 SP1 x64 の ISO から作ります。
scripts/setup.sh --shell win7 --media /path/to/Windows7SP1x64.iso
ログイン画面でセッション「Windows 7 Shell (Wine, X11)」を選びます。
詳しい手順とオプションは 🔗 導入手順（INSTALL.md） にあります。Wine をソースからビルドするので、4 コアで 1 時間半ほどかかります。 テーマ（XP のクラシックなど）と文字の大きさは、後から変えられます（見た目と文字の大きさを変える）。
Warning
- Windows XP（と Windows 7）の ISO はご自身で入手してください。 このリポジトリにも導入スクリプトにも、Microsoft のファイルを 取得する処理はありません。ISO と取り出したファイルの扱いは、Microsoft の使用許諾に従ってください。
- 利用は自己責任でお願いします。 データの損失や不具合について、作者は責任を負いません。
- Microsoft とも Wine プロジェクトとも関係のない、非公式のプロジェクトです。
- 確かめているのは日本語版と英語版の XP SP3（x86）だけです。ほかの言語の XP も英語版と同じ設定で入れるので動くかもしれませんが、
一切試していません（setup.sh は警告を出して続けます）。
LightDM ─ XP のようこそ画面 (greeter/)
   └─ XP Shell セッション (session/supervisor.py)
        ├─ Wine 11.0 + 151 本のパッチ (wine/patches/)
        │    └─ XP の explorer.exe, shell32.dll, …（ISO から取り出したもの。ReactOS や Windows 7 のシェルではそれらのもの）
        ├─ bridge-wm: X11 のウィンドウマネージャー + Win32 の代理ウィンドウ (bridge-wm/)
        │    （Wayland のセッションでは、ウィンドウマネージャーの代わりにパッチを当てた labwc。wayland/）
        └─ fcitx5 + Mozc, トレイの仲介 (bridge-wm/tray.py)
仕組みや設計の詳しい説明は docs/ にまとめています。
- loss32: Wine の上の Win32 のソフトウェアだけでデスクトップを作る Linux ディストリビューションの計画です。 ReactOS の部品も使います。win4wine が XP 本物のシェルを Debian の上で動かすのに対し、loss32 は自由なソフトウェアだけで作ります。
- Windows 由来のバイナリには手を加えません。違いは Wine とその周辺で吸収します。
- Microsoft のバイナリを逆アセンブルしません。挙動は公開 API と、実際の XP の上で動かす自作のプローブで調べています。
- Microsoft のファイル、取り出したもの、Wine の prefix は、Git 管理外の localres/ と .local/ にだけ置きます。
- AshesTom さん（フォーク）: XP の画面のプロパティ、
サウンド、キーボードの配列、通知領域の XP のアイコン、スタートメニューの左の列、Internet Explorer 6 と Windows Media Player 9、
起動中のようこそ画面、タイトルバーのアニメーションと小さいアイコン、Arch Linux への対応、xp.sh など。
LGPL-2.1-or-later（Wine と同じ）です。対象はこのリポジトリのコードとパッチだけです。
ただし wayland/patches/labwc/ は labwc と同じ GPL-2.0-only、wayland/patches/wlroots/ は wlroots と同じ MIT です。
Windows XP と Windows 7 のファイルと、スクリーンショットに写っている XP と Windows 7 の画面の著作権は Microsoft にあります。
ReactOS のシェルで使う ReactOS のファイルは、ReactOS のライセンス（GPL-2.0-or-later、DLL の多くは LGPL-2.1-or-later）に従います。

articles.title: You can't afford to keep your SSH keys on disk
articles.body:
You can't afford to keep your SSH keys on disk
Although it's clear to me that some of the panic is unwarranted, all the recent security vulnerability reports and company breaches are a good reason to think about what you're doing to avoid risk, and to mitigate exposure if something bad happens.
I'm a pathological self-hoster and I've been running all kinds of systems, from old toy projects to fun tools, and over time I've accumulated a lot of them. This has changed in the last couple of months, where I've instead been pruning my running services. I've taken down unused old apps, because anything can be an entry point into your system. And they were unused anyway. I've also moved most of services behind my Tailscale, with some judicious use of tailscale funnel to poke little holes for specific things that do need to be publicly accessible. And I've been obssessively updating everything on my servers that can be updated.
That brings us to my personal computer. I've been trying to do the same kind of due diligence that I did for my servers, on my personal devices. I have been a long time user of password managers, and I recently wrote about moving to Bitwarden, and I am careful to always enable 2FA or passkeys on every service I use. But one area I've fallen behind is SSH keys.
A better approach to SSH keys
I was keeping copies of my private keys in my password manager, for safe-keeping, but I was still using the version on disk, loaded into memory with ssh-add. To just make this absolutely clear, this means that the private keys are vulnerable to be exiltrated by malicious code scanning my disk. After reading articles like I deleted all my SSH keys, I finally decided to take the next step and get them off disk.
I knew that for this to work for me, it had to be easy to use and the disruption had to be minimal, and so although things like the OSX Secure Enclave sounds incredibly cool, I needed something with better ergonomics. I already had Bitwarden set up, with the keys in it, and so that's the approach I ended up taking, and it has worked great for me.
Setting up the Bitwarden SSH agent
Ok, let's go through the steps. First, make sure your private keys are in Bitwarden. If they are not, you'll want to import them. Note that the Bitwarden UI for importing SSH keys is a bit awkward.
- Create a new SSH key in Bitwarden, it'll automatically generate one for you.
- Copy your existing private key into your clipboard, eg cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | pbcopy.
- On the Private Key header in the edit form, at the very far right of the asterisks hiding the value, there's an upload icon, click it.
- Your private key has been imported. Give it a good name and save.
Once you're done with that, you can now move on to the next step, which is enabling the Bitwarden SSH agent. Note that these instructions are for the direct install, if you installed it through the App Store I think the path is different. Go to Preferences, App settings (all accounts), and find the checkbox for "Enable SSH agent". You'll also get the option of choosing how often it prompts you for permission, when something wants to use the key. I went for whenever the vault is locked, which I have set to every 4 hours, balancing security with convenience.
Next, add to your ~/.ssh/config file:
Host *
  IdentityAgent ~/.bitwarden-ssh-agent.sock
This tells ssh to use the Bitwarden SSH agent. This applies globally, so anything that calls ssh should now check the agent. Separately, you'll want to add this to your terminal config file, eg .zshrc:
export SSH_AUTH_SOCK=~/.bitwarden-ssh-agent.sock
This ensures anything that needs the SSH agent in your terminal, that isn't ssh, also go to the right place. This covers tools like ssh-keygen. Okay, now try it out with ssh-add -L. This should list all the keys loaded into ssh-agent. If you're confident you've copied all of your keys into your password manager, you can now delete the ones on disk.
Bonus: git commit signing
Git commits traditionally contain author information, but no proof that the author is who they say they are. This means it's trivial to impersonate someone else in a commit. It's still mitigated by the fact that git repositories generally have access controls, so a third party would not be able to push commits in the first place, but there is also a mechanism available for proving that the git originated from the claimed author: commit signing.
In the past, this was limited to GPG keys, but modern git supports signing using SSH keys. So I've set this up too, using a dedicated key that only has that job. This means that creating the commit and pushing it to the repo requires two separate SSH keys, and each one has to be authorized separately.
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey "key::$(ssh-add -L | grep 'YOURKEYNAME')"
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global tag.gpgsign true
Go to a repo and create a commit, then run git cat-file -p HEAD, and you should see your signature there.
To have forges recognize your signature you have to teach them what it is. For Github that means going to https://github.com/settings/keys and adding it as a signing key. Tangled automatically trusts your configured SSH keys as signing keys. Gitea and Forgejo require some extra steps to trust your key, just follow their instructions at /user/settings/keys.
My experience after a couple of weeks
I've adjusted quickly. Everything just works out of the box, the only added friction is that now and then Bitwarden prompts me for permission to use keys, which if it's unlocked just means clicking "approve" on a dialog. If it's locked, I can unlock it with touch ID.
If any Bitwarden employees happen to be reading this, it would be nice if instead of clicking approve, I could use touch ID to approve use of the key. Or at least by hitting enter. As it is, I always have to move to the touchpad to approve. It would also be great if I could separately configure the vault lock interval and the same interval for keys. But that's just minor requests, overall it works just great for me, and it's not too disruptive.
And now I get to sleep a bit easier!
Written by Johanna Larsson. Thoughts on this post? Find me on Bluesky at @jola.dev .
Related posts
Proposal for Tranquil PDS: Type-safe scopes
Tranquil is a popular AT protocol PDS implementation. This is a proposal to introduce a type-safe building block for representing scopes.
Building an atproto account typeahead search service
Tern is a single binary atproto account typeahead, covering both display names and handles, with near instant updates.
Tangled in a box
What if you could run your own Tangled on a private network, behind Tailscale, or locally.

articles.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
articles.body:
Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.
xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel
module (xnu.ko) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS
processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its
memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (fki.ko).
With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the
desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.
One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (sw_vers, the Darwin kernel, launchd,
WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,
Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in).
Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.
The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).
Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the
hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (GPU=auto).
Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia): hosted macOS 27 running with
4 CPUs and 8 GiB of RAM (CPU rendering), shown over macOS Screen Sharing alongside an SSH session from the DGX Spark
host into the hosted Darwin userspace.
Inside the hosted macOS on DGX Spark: About This Mac (Chip: Unknown, 7.80 GB memory, macOS Golden Gate 27.2)
alongside sysctl machdep.cpu (ARM processor, hw.cpufamily: 0, hw.ncpu: 4) and hw.optional.arm.

   ↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)
 xnu.ko   (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)
   ↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)
 fki.ko   (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)
 Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)
- CPUs: each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host
(idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of
XNU code to XNU's handlers.
- Memory: XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).
- Devices: kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a
keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.
- GPU: Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux
host's GPU through the DRM bridge (kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using
Mesa's Venus driver; without a supported DRM bridge backend it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.
Working on two arm64 Linux setups:
- Apple Silicon Mac in an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit, 1 to 6 hosted CPUs):
  - macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s).
  - Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes, Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.
  - Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each
run's log kept in /var/log/xnulinux/.
  - The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU (Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max)) and is enabled by default
(GPU=auto) when a virtio-gpu render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering (GPU=off) otherwise.
- Bare-metal NVIDIA DGX Spark (Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia):
  - Boots to the full macOS desktop (Screen Sharing and SSH working) directly on bare-metal arm64 Linux with CPUS=4 and 8 GiB of RAM reserved for XNU.
  - Currently renders on the CPU (Mesa lavapipe, GPU=off): xnudrmd only forwards virtio-gpu (Venus) ioctls today,
so hardware GPU pass-through on the GB10 GPU requires a new DRM bridge backend.
What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md. Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into
the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).
- An arm64 Linux host with PAC (FEAT_PAuth), 4K pages, and at least 16 GB of RAM (8 GB reserved for the hosted
kernel). Tested on:
  - NVIDIA DGX Spark (bare-metal Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS aarch64, Linux 7.0.0-1025-nvidia; CPU rendering for now).
  - Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit for GPU access via virtio-gpu Venus, or tart).
- A Mac with Xcode to make the system disk and build the GPU parts.
- A macOS 27 installation (an Apple Virtualization VM disk) of your own. No Apple binaries are in this repository or distributed by it: the kexts Apple ships, the macOS system disk and its trust cache come from your own installation.
- scripts/vm-xnu-build.sh (on the arm64 Linux host, once): sets up the macOS-DroidVM Linux toolchain and builds XNU
(xnu-12377.121.6) natively on arm64.
- scripts/vm-xnu-rebuild.sh: applies xnu-patches/, builds the kernel and kexts/, and links the kernel collection
with Apple's kexts from your macOS installation.
- scripts/mk-macvm-disk.sh (on the Mac): turns a macOS VM disk made by Apple's installer into the hosted system's disk
and copies it into the Linux VM.
- scripts/xnulinux-boot.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): builds fki.ko and xnu.ko against the running kernel, brings
up the network (and the GPU bridge when there is a render node) and boots the hosted system. Its console is scripts/xnu-console.sh, its screen tools/hosted/fb2png.py, input tools/hosted/xnu-input.py. On a bare-metal
host (such as a DGX Spark), set the carve-out (mem=, carve_base=, carve_mb=) to fit the machine's physical
memory layout, and set GPU=off (xnudrmd supports only virtio-gpu for now).
- scripts/install-service.sh (on the arm64 Linux host): runs it as xnulinux.service, configured in /etc/xnulinux.conf (CPUs, memory, disk, GPU). On the Mac, scripts/install-krun-agent.sh keeps the VM itself
running.
- GPU (optional, on the Mac): gpu/venus/build-darwin.sh builds the hosted Vulkan driver, gpu/xnu-cpu-metal/ the
Metal plugin (see its README).
The Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an
SPDX-License-Identifier; the license texts are in LICENSES/.
xnu.ko is on the XNU side of the line: it runs XNU's code in its own address space, so it is APSL-2.0 like XNU, and
Linux reports it as a non-GPL module (MODULE_LICENSE("Proprietary"), which taints the kernel as ZFS does). It must not
include Linux headers beyond the module ABI, call Linux functions other than fki_*, or carry Linux code. Upstream code
(XNU, macOS-DroidVM's toolchain, Mesa, metal2vulkan, the Vulkan loader, LLVM) is fetched at pinned revisions and patched at
build time; it is never committed.
- macOS-DroidVM and UniXNU: the 4K-page XNU base, the Linux-hosted XNU toolchain, and the display, Ethernet and input kexts these are derived from.
- metal2vulkan, Mesa (Venus, lavapipe), virglrenderer and krunkit.
- Apple's open-source XNU.

articles.title: 'It's greed': Zohran Mamdani blasts Amazon over new $5 fee hike in NYC
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.  
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is taking aim at Amazon over a warning the online retail giant has been flashing at New Yorkers as they shop: Their orders could soon cost as much as $5 more.  
"Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds $5 to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe," Mamdani wrote in a Nov. 19 post on X (1). "It's greed."  
Top Picks  
Amazon is fighting a proposed New York City law (2) that would overhaul how the company gets packages from its warehouses to your doorstep. And now the giant seems to be recruiting its own customers to help fight that legislative battle.  
The company has begun displaying warnings on its website and in its shopping app, directing customers to contact their local lawmakers and oppose the legislation.  
For Americans who have come to depend on the convenience of online shopping, the prospect of paying more every time they click "buy" is hardly welcome news. But how much of Amazon's warning should shoppers take at face value?  
Why Amazon is threatening to raise prices  
Introduced in February by New York City Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán, the Delivery Protection Act (3) would require companies operating certain delivery facilities to directly employ most of their warehouse and delivery workers rather than outsource those jobs to third-party contractors.  
The legislation would also establish a $500 annual licensing fee per facility, mandatory worker safety training and additional protections against unfair dismissal.  
Amazon contends that complying with the legislation could make its existing delivery model economically untenable in New York City, potentially forcing it to relocate operations beyond city limits.  
The company has cited research from consulting firm AKRF estimating additional annual household costs of between $409 and $664. However, Amazon hasn't established precisely how those figures translate into a $5 increase per order, per Fox Business (4).  
And the bill, which remains in committee, hasn't passed yet.  
            Read More: Millionaires under 45 hold only 32% of their wealth in stocks. Here's where their money is actually going  
How much is convenience costing you?  
An extra $5 might seem inconsequential when you're ordering $100 worth of household essentials. But if you order from Amazon twice a week, that potential increase amounts to $520 a year.  
A big pill to swallow for Americans caught in escalating financial struggles, especially those already paying $139 annually for Amazon Prime — no doubt in part for its free shipping.  
Whether you live in New York City or elsewhere in the country, it's worth taking stock of what you're paying for convenience. Between retail memberships, food delivery subscriptions and expedited shipping, you could be spending hundreds of dollars a year before accounting for the actual goods you're buying.  
For retirees living on fixed incomes or workers trying to catch up on their retirement savings, that's money that could be put to better use.  
A quick daily check-in of your accounts can show you exactly where your money is going.  
An app like Rocket Money can easily flag recurring subscriptions, upcoming bills and unusual charges by pulling in transactions from all your linked accounts.  
This can help you cut unnecessary costs so you can manually redirect savings straight into your retirement fund. No spreadsheets, no guesswork, no stress. Small habits like this can make a big difference over time.  
Rocket Money's intuitive app offers a variety of free and premium tools. Free features include subscription tracking, bill reminders and budgeting basics, while premium features — like automated savings, net worth tracking, customizable dashboards and more — make it easier to stay on top of your retirement contributions and overall financial goals.  
You don't necessarily have to give up online shopping, either. Waiting until you have several items to order, choosing slower shipping when it's cheaper, or picking up your purchases at a nearby store can help trim your expenses.  
If those changes free up even $10 a week, consider setting that money aside to build an emergency fund that can cushion your household against future price increases.  
A high-yield account like a Wealthfront Cash Account can be a great place to grow your uninvested cash, offering both competitive interest rates and easy access to your money when you need it.  
A Wealthfront Cash Account currently offers a base rate APY of 3.55% through program banks. With a new client boost and direct deposit incentive, referred clients can earn up to a 4.55% APY.  
That's about 10 times the national deposit savings rate, according to the FDIC's November report (5).  
With no minimum balances or account fees, as well as 24/7 withdrawals and free domestic wire transfers, your funds remain accessible at all times. Plus, you get access to up to $8M FDIC Insurance eligibility through program banks.  
Make retailers pay you back  
When was the last time you compared the price of something on Amazon with what your local retailer charges?  
The convenience of having a package arrive at your doorstep tomorrow can make it tempting to skip comparison shopping altogether. And once you've paid for an annual retail membership, you may feel compelled to shop exclusively with that retailer to get your money's worth.  
Checking competing retailers' prices, factoring in shipping costs and taking advantage of free in-store pickup could help you keep more of your money.  
You can also be more selective about how you pay. If retailers are looking for ways to squeeze a few more dollars out of every transaction, there's no reason you shouldn't try to recover some of that money yourself.  
A big chunk of your monthly spending probably goes to the same few things: groceries, gas and a handful of subscriptions. Since you're paying for them anyway, putting those routine purchases on a cash back credit card is one way to get some of that money back.  
Many cards pay higher cash back in select categories like these. Say you spend $500 a month on groceries and gas and earn 3% back in those categories. That's $180 a year for purchases you'd make anyway.  
Just keep in mind that rewards only pay off if you clear your balance each month. Card balances that carry interest averaged a 22.36% APR in August, according to the Federal Reserve, and at that rate, interest can quickly cancel out what you earn.  
Some of these cards come with extra perks, too. Many offer a welcome bonus once you hit a minimum spend in the first few months, and some pay higher cash back in select categories like groceries, gas or dining. A big purchase you were already planning could help you reach that bonus faster. Shop around to find a 0% intro APR card with perks that fit your spending habits.  
What To Read Next

articles.title: GL.iNet Security Notice 2026-11-20
articles.body:
Security Notice: GoodCloud Remote Management Incident
What happened and how we responded
Who is affected
What you should do now
For all users: install the security firmware
If unauthorized access is known or suspected: contain and recover
If your device connected to GoodCloud: replace potentially exposed passwords and keys
Download and install the security update
Router security firmware downloads
KVM security firmware downloads
Optional device checks before updating
First choice for broader coverage: community security check
Optional KVM check — limited coverage
Technical details and investigation findings
How the incident happened
Vulnerability reports and remediation coverage
Additional findings and recovery limits
- 
Separate router persistence reports. Community users reported a modified startup script and suspicious processes; GL.iNet acknowledged these reports in the forum. Some reported file dates predate November 20. The original reports do not establish the initial entry path or a connection to this incident. A process name alone is not proof of infection. Do not assume incident malware cleanup resolves every separate persistence finding.
- 
Why keeping settings can leave other changes.Community KVM testing reported that an added startup script and SSH key survived a configuration-preserving upgrade on a test RM1. This illustrates a recovery limit; it does not establish that every affected KVM had those modifications. For known or suspected compromise, reinstall without keeping configuration using the model's supported upgrade options.
- 
Firmware and boot integrity.Community recovery analysis explains that a normal reset or firmware reinstall may not rewrite every flash region. This is a recovery limitation, not evidence that boot components were changed in this attack. Contact Support if there are reasons to suspect deeper changes or activity persists after recovery.
-

articles.title: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $44 billion
articles.body:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday.
CrowdStrike and Zscaler said that the deal will create the “largest single addressable market” for cybersecurity, which will enable the companies to better position themselves for the AI era.
Zscaler is a San Jose, California-based tech company that provides cloud cybersecurity products to about 8,000 enterprise companies. The company offers zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each and every time they access an internal system or resource. The aim is to protect against hackers from stealing credentials and using them to gain unfettered access to a company’s network.
CrowdStrike, which secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a company’s network, said the deal will unite its endpoint protection software with Zscaler’s zero-trust platform to better defend their customers against data breaches. By combining the two products, CrowdStrike and Zscaler say that they can offer “superior protection” to their customers.
In remarks on Monday, the companies said that the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI.
The deal, which is subject to regulatory approval, is expected to close around this time next year.

articles.title: Yes, 17M lines of Lean is a lot
articles.body:
Yes, 17m lines of Lean is a lot
AI disclosure: I wrote all text here, but used Agent Duel (an open source battle system on top of OpenCode) to research sources of Lean proofs and generate charts.
The recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?
To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.
(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.)
Famous theorems in Mathlib
Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.
These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.
Every Lean package on Reservoir
Reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:
- 88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.
- 36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.
- 27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.
So yes, 17m lines is a lot.

articles.title: Nespresso's project to reduce grams of coffee per capsule
articles.body:
Introduction
The article is about Nespresso’s internal project to basically reduce the amount of grams per capsule that they produce. In August of 2026, I was informed by a Nespresso internal employee about “Project Olympus”. At first I didn’t think much of it and wasn’t sure how to deal with the information. It seems based on the docs that they were possibly improving the formulas, but I still questioned how that is possible with a reduction of grams of coffee.
The Documentation
The below text is the actual Project Olympus internal text for everyone’s reference to review:
PROJECT OLYMPUS: VERTUO
As part of our ongoing commitment to delivering an exceptional coffee experience, Nespresso is continuously innovating across every step of our process-while preserving the taste, quality, and consistency our consumers expect.
What’s changing?
Beginning in 2026, select Nespresso Vertuo coffee recipes will undergo a recipe optimization. Through advancements in grinding and roasting techniques, we’ve refined these recipes to achieve the same great taste and in-cup experience—using slightly less coffee per capsule.
This change will be rolled out gradually from Q1 through Q3 2026.
What’s staying the same?
While the capsule weight may be slightly reduced, the core elements of the coffee experience are unchanged:
- Same taste profile consumers know and love
- Same coffee volume per cup
- Same caffeine levels, with only minor natural variation
- Same high-quality standards across all affected coffees
These updates have been carefully validated from a sensory perspective to ensure no compromise in flavor or satisfaction.
Why are we optimizing recipes?
Innovation is at the heart of Nespresso. Our development teams are constantly exploring ways to improve how we roast and grind our coffees-while delivering the same consistent, high-quality results in every cup.
Project Olympus reflects this effort: a behind-the-scenes optimization designed to maintain excellence, even as we evolve our processes.
What if consumers ask questions?
In some cases, consumers may notice that certain capsules feel lighter than before or ask about possible changes. If inquiries arise, teams should emphasize:
- Our commitment to quality and customer satisfaction
- That the taste and experience remain the same
- That the update reflects process innovation, not a reduction in value
The approved reactive statement and Q&A from the Project Olympus FAQ should be used to guide responses.
- HQ development teams are continuously looking into innovating our coffee processes, whilst ensuring optimal and consistent in-cup quality.
- We have optimized the grinding and roasting processes of some of our coffees, which has resulted to a slightly reduced capsule weight while providing the same consumer experience coffee lovers expect from Nespresso.
WAVE 1: Projected transition in market Q1 2026
- Scope (6 SKUS): DOUBLE ESPRESSO SCURO, DOUBLE ESPRESSO CHIARO, DOUBLE ESPRESSO DOLCE, FORTADO, ORAFIO, RISTRETTO INTENSO
WAVE 2: Projected transition in market TBA
- Scope (8 SKUS): MELOZIO, STORMIO, ODACIO, MO COSTA RICA, MO COLOMBIA, BIANCO DOPPIO, SOLEILIO, ARONDIO
Review attached memo and FAQ for additional information. No action is required as of right now.
Officially Whistle Blowing
On/about Sepetember 5, 2026, I noticed a post on r/nespresso asking about whether Nespresso had changed their recipes:
I then decided to offically be the first whistle blower about Project Olympus. A large number of Nespresso consumers were definitely not happy with Nespresso’s decision to reduce the number of grams per capsule. There are many users that are seriously considering to drop Nespresso and move to alternative coffee options.
Coffee Capsules Affected
There are a number of people that have asked which coffees are affected, and that’s a resonable question. From what is currently being observed, almost all the range of coffees are being reduced. The only ones that don’t appear to be affected are Lungos for OL, and Alto XLs (and other larger coffees) for Vertuo.
You can always use my spreadsheet to track any of the coffees that have been affected by Project Olympus:
https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1kZJCdTmqQla2ha3DDYyixQDIUuf9wLvt3122akBkhgM/edit?usp=sharing
Below are screenshots of a spreadsheet showing the currently affected capsules (as of November 12, 2026) showing the percentage change:
Please go to my ko-fi buy me a coffee page at: https://ko-fi.com/alvinbunk to support and donate to me for writing coffee reviews. Thank you
!

articles.title: Samsung’s absurd 1,100Hz gaming monitor hits shelves next month for $899.99
articles.body:
After being teased in December 2025 and getting an arguably unnecessary pre-release spec bump in August, the Samsung Odyssey G6 G60H rolls out next month for $899.99. The 27-inch gaming monitor will have an absurd 1,100Hz refresh rate, narrowly edging out LG’s UltraGear 25G590B, which tops out at 1,000Hz.
Samsung’s absurd 1,100Hz gaming monitor hits shelves next month for $899.99
A year after being announced, the Odyssey G6 is finally being released.
Is there any value in these ultra-fast refresh rates? That’s up for debate. But whether or not you can actually see the difference, it does give the company bragging rights. So there is that, I guess.
The G60H will only be able ot hit 1,100Hz in 1080p. Bumping the resolution up to 1440p will drop the refresh rate to 600Hz, which is still absurdly fast. The Dual Mode IPS panel is also the first to feature Samsung’s new Odyssey Clear Motion tech, which reduces motion blur during games. Eventually, the company plans to bring Clear Motion to more gaming monitors. Black Equalizer also makes it easier to see details in dark scenes.
Beyond that, the G60H also supports HDR10+, Nvidia G-Sync, and AMD FreeSync Premium.

articles.title: Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures
articles.body:
Microsoft Admits Some Emails Bounced During Global Outlook Outage, Reveals New Failures (neowin.net) 14
			
		 	
				After millions lost access to Microsoft 365 services (including Outlook) on November 12, Microsoft "has published the final post-incident report," writes Neowin, "and it reveals that some emails were never delivered to their intended recipients."
"The report also details previously undisclosed failures affecting Microsoft's email security features..."
   Microsoft confirmed that all queued enterprise emails were eventually delivered and that it found no enterprise messages that were permanently lost. However, it is not the same with Outlook consumer users. The company acknowledged that some delayed messages destined for consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days expired, and senders received non-delivery reports. Microsoft did not reveal how many emails were affected or how many users received non-delivery reports.
The final report also reveals that the outage disrupted several important email security capabilities in Microsoft Defender for Office. For example, the Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) feature, which automatically removes malicious emails after delivery, was delayed because updated threat intelligence was unavailable. This means affected messages may not have been removed as quickly as usual. Microsoft also confirmed that users experienced problems opening URLs protected by Safe Links. Depending on their organization's security policies, some users may have encountered a "Skip verification" option when Safe Links attempted to check a URL...
Microsoft also acknowledged that its first customer notification arrived approximately 20 minutes after the widespread impact began. It plans to improve automated outage notifications by the end of 2026 to improve communication. 
"Microsoft eventually restored the services about 12 hours later..."

articles.title: My trusty 27-inch Alienware QD-OLED gaming monitor is just $280
articles.body:
Alienware’s AW2726DM QD-OLED gaming monitor was a great deal even at its original $349.99 price. The low price and impressive specs were enough to convince me to get one at launch, and I’m glad that I did. I’m a little jealous that you have the opportunity to save $70 on the monitor I’ve been using for work and play for several months. Best Buy and Dell are selling the 27-inch 1440p monitor for $279.99 ahead of Black Friday.
My trusty 27-inch Alienware QD-OLED gaming monitor is just $280

articles.title: Nothing’s upcoming Ear Note is a pair of earbuds with AI transcription
articles.body:
Nothing’s new AI device is the Ear Note, a set of earbuds and their microphone-equipped charging case that can record and transcribe conversations, with a connected app to manage the recordings, transcriptions and AI-generated summaries, similar to Apple’s new Watch feature and devices like Amazon’s Bee wearable. Nothing CEO Carl Pei demonstrated the new device to Bloomberg, but said the company hasn’t yet settled on a price ahead of a planned launch on December 8th.
Nothing’s upcoming Ear Note is a pair of earbuds with AI transcription
The new AI device from Nothing can record and transcribe audio with AI from the earbuds or via microphones on their charging case.
The report also says Nothing’s rumored plans for an AI smartwatch and smart glasses are delayed, while it will be “pursuing a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year than it did in 2026.” In a post on X, Pei said this is “the first of many products building a hardware context layer for AI. Rather than ask you to carry a new product, we took something you already wear and trust and made it intelligent.”
According to Bloomberg, the earbuds will “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations.” Users will also be able to record themselves with a “Talk” button on the case, like Nothing previously included on the Ear 3, which also has recording capabilities. Earlier this year, Nothing introduced an Audio Snapshot recording feature in the Ear 3A. Anker’s Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro Max can also record directly to the earbuds’ case and generate AI transcripts and summaries in an app.

articles.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
articles.body:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.
I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)
Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.
This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.
We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!
The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.

articles.title: Ladybird is now in alpha
articles.body:
Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux.
I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^)
Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional.
This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details.
We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird!
The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that.
If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol.
Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

articles.body:
Dance into the Week with an Entirely Hand-Drawn Animation for the Osees
Catherine Lepage will have you leaping out of your desk chair with her self-directed “Dancing on Osees.” The irresistible animation features a quirky troupe of characters who can’t help but get down to “Together Tomorrow.” As the energetic track bolts forward, so do the hand-drawn dancers, who Lepage captures through stop-motion collages on paper.
The Montréal-based artist graciously shares glimpses behind the scenes on Instagram.

articles.title: The next circle of security hell
articles.body:
A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare”. Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness.
Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point.
The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why.
In the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match users’ expectations.
In the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and users will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying.
I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up.
What happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning.

articles.title: CollectWise (YC F24) Is Hiring
articles.body:
Automating consumer debt collection with AI
About Us
CollectWise is a fast-growing and well-funded Y Combinator-backed startup. We’re using generative AI to automate debt collection, a $35B market in the US alone. Our AI agents are already outperforming human collectors by 2X, and we’re doing so at a fraction of the cost.
With a small team, we scaled to a $3M annualized revenue run rate in just over a year, and we’re now hiring a Founding Customer Success Manager to help us reach $10M+ over the next year.
The Role
We’re looking for a Founding Customer Success Manager to own customer relationships after launch, drive revenue expansion, and ensure customers are successful with CollectWise.
You’ll work at the intersection of customer success, account management, and operations, managing customer communication, resolving technical issues, optimizing AI agents, monitoring performance, and growing revenue from existing customers.
This is a highly hands-on role. You should be comfortable managing multiple customer relationships, proactively identifying opportunities to improve customer outcomes, making adjustments to AI agents and workflows, collaborating with engineering to resolve more complex issues, and growing revenue across your accounts by increasing platform usage and expanding customers into additional products and use cases.
Your success will be measured by customer satisfaction, retention, revenue expansion, product adoption, and customer performance.
Responsibilities
Own day-to-day customer relationships after customers have gone live, serving as their primary point of contact
Troubleshoot and resolve customer issues by adjusting configurations, coordinating solutions, and escalating technical issues to engineering when necessary
Drive revenue growth across existing accounts by executing upsell and cross-sell opportunities, increasing platform usage, and expanding customers into additional products and use cases
Monitor customer usage, performance, and trends to identify opportunities to improve results, increase adoption, and reduce churn
Continuously optimize customer AI agents, prompts, workflows, and outreach strategies to improve performance
Communicate technical issues clearly to customers and internal engineering teams, coordinating resolutions and keeping customers informed throughout the process
Build strong customer relationships through regular check-ins, performance reviews, and proactive communication, including preparing reports and presentations to demonstrate results and recommend improvements
Support new implementations, additional use cases, and product rollouts for existing customers
Assist with customer onboarding and operational requirements, including completing vendor diligence questionnaires related to security, compliance, and company operations
Desired Qualifications
Compensation
CollectWise is revolutionizing debt recovery with autonomous AI agents and an integrated legal network. We boost recovery rates, reduce costs, and maintain a positive brand image through respectful, data-driven interactions.

articles.title: Localcode, open source agentic coding on your Mac with one command
articles.body:
Agentic coding. Local models. On your Mac.
uv pip install localcode
Upgrade with uv pip install -U localcode.
cd your-project
localcode
To use the running model from another local app, open /server or run localcode api for its
OpenAI compatible endpoint. See the Local API guide.
- Reads and edits files in your project
- Runs your tests, builds, Git and shell commands inside the project on its own, and asks before touching anything outside it
- Searches code by name, content or structure
- Scaffolds and launches apps, then checks that they respond
- Remembers the task across messages
- Mac with Apple Silicon, macOS 13 or newer
- 16 GB unified memory or more
- Python 3.10 or newer
- Disk space for LocalCode and your chosen model (download sizes below)
Choose from 12 models and 169 quant options for coding, image input and typed decisions. Models download from Hugging Face. Downloads run in parallel and can resume if interrupted. Switch with /models. LocalCode recommends the most capable one that fits your Mac's memory and marks it with a star.
Speed: Gemma 4, Qwen 3.6, Muse Glimmer and Qwen 3.8 draft tokens with the vendor's own speculative drafter, which downloads with the model. The model server's GPU kernels ship precompiled, so the first start after an install is quicker.
What LocalCode adds on top of the stock model server to make local models faster and better at coding.
Speed
- Drafting: the vendor's own drafter guesses tokens ahead (about 2x faster replies on Gemma 4, Qwen 3.6, Qwen 3.8 and Muse Glimmer)
- Copy drafting: when the model rewrites a file it already read, it copies instead of generating (3.5 to 4x faster on rewrites)
- Prompt cache reuse: the system prompt stays the same every turn, so the model only reads what is new
- Warm-up: the first request's prompt is read while the model loads, so your first message starts sooner
- Precompiled GPU kernels: no half-minute shader compile on first start
- Threads matched to your Mac's performance cores
- Flash attention on by default
- Inkling 2: its experts run on the GPU (were silently on the CPU, about 5x slower), banded attention and a fused activation op halve its GPU memory and read prompts 20 to 30% faster
- Downloads run in parallel, resume if interrupted, and keep going while you use another model
Memory
- 8-bit KV cache by default: half the memory of full precision, so longer context fits
- Inkling 2 uses a 16-bit cache instead: its attention reads it directly, so long prompts read 1.4 to 1.8x faster and it needs 3.3 GB less memory at 128K context
- Context sized from what the server reports, so long chats compact before they run out of room
- The picker recommends the most capable model that fits your Mac
Quality
- Hidden thinking off by default, so answers come straight away; a model that gets stuck thinking is recovered instead of failing
- Plan panel: the model keeps a task list and is reminded to update it
- Stuck detection: a model that makes no progress, or keeps failing the same check, is nudged to change approach and then stopped so it reports what it has
- Every release is tested live on every model (load, reply, tool calls, images) before it ships
Inference is local. Three features use the network: model downloads, the web_search and web_fetch tools, and any MCP servers you add. See Network Boundary for the full list.
Powerful, personal AI should work for everyone, on any device, anywhere. That means running it locally. localcode is a first step.
To sponsor localcode, reach out.
See CONTRIBUTING.md.
Apache 2.0. See LICENSE.

articles.title: GLP-1 drugs could have a surprisingly large environmental payoff
articles.body:
GLP-1 weight-loss medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy could affect much more than the waistlines of the people who take them. If widely used, our new research suggests these appetite-suppressing medicines could transform the global food system and free up vast areas of agricultural land.
The global food system is ultimately driven by demand. If people eat less, producers respond, affecting production, prices, trade and how much land is needed. We used a powerful computer simulation to explore scenarios ranging from GLP-1 use concentrated in high-income countries to widespread global access.
With widespread use of these medicines among adults living with obesity, we estimate that reduced calorie intake could prevent up to 6.6 million deaths each year by 2050, while freeing up as much as 32 million hectares of agricultural land – an area slightly larger than Italy – for other uses.
The biggest effects, however, occurred when reduced calorie intake was combined with a shift towards healthier diets. In this scenario, up to 7 million deaths could be avoided each year by 2050, while around 46 million hectares of agricultural land would have become available for other uses. This suggests that alongside weight-loss medicines, we need to make healthier options more widely available, affordable and more appealing.
The food system could respond in unexpected ways
Food systems are interconnected across countries. If demand falls in one part of the world, this can affect farming, trade and food prices elsewhere, with consequences for people who are not taking the medications at all.
Lower demand from GLP-1 users, for instance, could make food cheaper. That sounds positive, but cheaper food could also encourage greater consumption among non-users, offsetting some of the intended benefit. The effects of widespread GLP-1 use, in other words, cannot be understood just by looking at individual patients’ weight loss. They ripple through the global food system.
It’s tempting to read these findings as an argument for putting more people on weight-loss medication. That would miss the bigger picture.
Obesity has often been framed as a “lifestyle disease”, blaming individual people for not having enough willpower. But diets are shaped by what food is available, what it costs, how it’s marketed, where shops are located and what’s most convenient. In many high-income countries, it is remarkably easy to consume large amounts of cheap, energy-dense food. Society tells people to make healthier choices while surrounding them with an environment that often encourages the opposite.
The UK government commissioned national food strategy, finalised in 2021, made this point clearly: improving diets can’t simply be about asking individuals to choose better. The wider food environment needs to change to make the better choice the easy one.
Our findings shouldn’t be taken to mean that people living with obesity have a responsibility to lose weight to reduce the environmental impacts of food production. Rather, our research examines the wider consequences that changes in food demand could have across the food system.
Changing the food system alongside medicine
A healthier diet is not necessarily just a diet with fewer calories. It could mean more fruit, vegetables and other nutritious foods, alongside less excessive consumption of foods linked to poor health. These changes affect not only human health but also agriculture, land use and the environment.
Rather than asking whether GLP-1 medications or healthier diets are the answer, let’s ask how they can work together. Imagine a food system where healthier foods are affordable and accessible, unhealthy options aren’t relentlessly promoted, agricultural policy supports nutritious and sustainable production, and people who need medical treatment can access it. That combination could be far more powerful than any single intervention.
GLP-1 medicines can play an important role in tackling obesity, but they shouldn’t become a technological fix that allows the wider food system to escape scrutiny. They can help people eat less in an unhealthy food environment, but the long-term goal should be to make it easier and more affordable to have a healthier, more sustainable diet.
The remarkable thing about GLP-1 medications may not be that they change how much food people eat. It may be that they show us, with new clarity, just how closely human health, food production and environmental health are connected, and how much could be gained if we tackled all three together.
